title: HEAR IT: Mom's frantic 911 call after thief steals Instacart driver's car with toddler inside
summary: Body camera video and 911 audio reveal the frantic 15-minute rescue of a 2-year-old from a stolen car during an Instacart delivery in Atlanta.
story: Body camera video captures the tense moments officers surround a stolen vehicle and arrest the suspect accused of driving away with a 2-year-old child still inside. Credit: Atlanta Police Department

A routine Instacart delivery turned into every parent's nightmare after a Georgia mother's car was stolen with her 2-year-old daughter still inside, as newly released 911 audio and police body camera video capture the frantic rescue.
"Someone just stole my car and it has my 2-year-old daughter in it," the distraught mother tells an Atlanta 911 dispatcher in audio released by police.

Atlanta police officers surround a stolen vehicle after tracking it down with license plate readers during the rescue of a 2-year-old girl. (Atlanta Police Department)
Moments later, she cries out again, "My daughter was inside!"
The ordeal unfolded around 4:36 p.m. on July 30, according to the Atlanta Police Department.
Police said the vehicle had been left running with the toddler inside while her mother delivered an Instacart order.
LICENSE PLATE CAMERAS ARE TRACKING DRIVERS EVERYWHERE

Officers with the department's Auto Crimes Enforcement Unit immediately began searching for the vehicle and used the city's license plate readers to locate the car, the suspect and the child in under 15 minutes, according to police.
Body camera video released by the department shows officers surrounding the stolen vehicle and ordering the driver to raise his hands and get out.
"Hands up! Hands up!" an officer shouts.

"Hands on the window now," another officer orders. "What you're gonna do is you're going to get out and face away from me, you understand me? Get out the car, slow. Put your hands behind your back."
The video shows officers taking the suspect into custody as the toddler cries nearby and her mother works to calm her.
"It's okay, baby. It's okay, baby," the mother can be heard saying.
Moments later, an officer radios, "The child is okay. The child's okay."
Police identified the suspect as 21-year-old Saleem Martin.
Mugshot of Saleem Martin, who faces kidnapping and other charges after police say he stole a vehicle with a toddler inside. (Atlanta Police Department)
Martin was charged with kidnapping, theft by taking, simple battery, entering an automobile, cruelty to children and criminal attempt to commit a felony, according to police.
Authorities said the toddler was unharmed and reunited with her parents.
According to an arrest warrant obtained by Atlanta NBC affiliate 11Alive, the child's mother later noticed that the bottom of her daughter's dress was unbuttoned.
The warrant alleges the toddler told her mother "the man did it," referring to the man who had been driving the car.
Martin allegedly had both hands on the child's torso when officers found him and was trying to duck down and hide between the seats, according to the warrant cited by the outlet.
The Atlanta Police Department's Special Victims Unit was brought into the investigation.
Martin allegedly told investigators he had been touching the child because he was trying to calm her down, according to 11Alive.

title: Renewed patriotism and career opportunities fuel Army's biggest recruiting surge in years
summary: Retention and recruiting goals are being exceeded as young Americans pursue Army careers in engineering, military intelligence and helicopter mechanics.
story: Fox News gets exclusive access inside Fort Hood as Brooke Taylor reports the latest on the military recruitment surge.

The U.S. Army has already reached its fiscal year 2026 active-duty recruiting goal months ahead of schedule, marking a dramatic turnaround after years of falling short as military leaders point to renewed patriotism, career opportunities and a growing sense of purpose among young Americans choosing to serve.

Fox News was granted exclusive access inside Fort Hood, one of the Army’s largest installations, where commanders and soldiers offered a firsthand look at what they say is driving the recruiting resurgence.

Just a few years ago, the Army was struggling to meet its recruiting goals. After hitting a low in fiscal year 2022, recruiting has climbed every year since, rising nearly 38% overall, with the biggest jump coming in fiscal year 2025. This fiscal year, the Army has already met its active-duty recruiting goal with more than 61,500 future soldiers signing on for service.
FIRST ON FOX: TRUMP TO OPEN DIRECT LINE WITH MILITARY FAMILIES IN GROUND-UP READINESS PUSH
The recruiting surge has been accompanied by another encouraging trend for Army leaders: retention goals are also being exceeded, with more soldiers choosing to continue their military careers.
(U.S. Army photo by Robin Hicks)
Among them is infantryman Guadalupe Campos, who joined the Army when he was 18 years old and recently extended his service nearly six years later.
"I wanted to do my due diligence and service to my country," Campos told Fox News.
TRUMP GIVES EMOTIONAL TRIBUTE TO FALLEN ARMY LT TYLER FEEHAN AFTER FLYING GRIEVING FAMILY ON AIR FORCE ONE
For Campos, serving in uniform has reinforced both his patriotism and the bonds formed alongside fellow soldiers.
"I love my country, I love America. This is our home, and we have, I mean, this is everything that we all have in common is this American flag that we fly on our right shoulder," he said.
(U.S. Army photo by Robin Hicks)
Campos said the Army brought together people from every walk of life, united by one common mission.
TRUMP IS PROVING THAT THE WAY TO BETTER OUR MILITARY IS TO SECURE OUR SUPPLY CHAINS

"A lot of the guys that I worked with, they come from a lot of parts of life, whether it’s good or bad. And at the end of the day, we have that one common goal and that’s to be ready when the time comes for us to have to do our jobs," he said. "We serve and protect the United States Constitution and its people from enemies of a foreign and domestic, and we take that to heart."
Jade Root, Army Recruiting battalion commander, said the recent turnaround reflects a broader desire among young Americans to serve.

"Locally we have seen a strong sense of young men and women who want to serve a purpose much higher than themselves. They understand the opportunities that the Army provides to acquire critical skills and leadership skills that will last them a lifetime," Root told Fox News.
U.S. Army helicopters fly past the Washington Monument and over the Great American State Fair on the National Mall in Washington, D.C., on July 3, 2026. (Andrew Leyden/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Root also believes the recruiting numbers reflect something larger.
"I think it shows a strong signal that patriotism is alive and well," Rood said. "We have a high propensity of people that want to serve, but most importantly that our Army is growing."
Army leaders say today’s recruits are motivated by a combination of patriotism, benefits and a sense of purpose.

The Army says today’s typical recruit is about 23 years old, and recruiters are spending more time in high schools, on college campuses and in local communities to connect with potential future soldiers.
"I always ask our recruiters, remember they are not just a number, this is someone’s son or daughter," Root said.

Today’s Army also extends far beyond traditional combat roles, offering more than 200 career fields, ranging from medics and helicopter mechanics to cybersecurity, engineering, military intelligence and animal care.
Army Animal Care Specialist Grizel Cornejo said many prospective recruits are surprised by the range of career opportunities available while serving.

As modern warfare continues to evolve, Army leaders say they’re increasingly looking for recruits with technical skills in areas such as cybersecurity, engineering and military intelligence as the service prepares for the future battlefield.

For commanders at Fort Hood, the recruiting rebound is about more than reaching a numerical goal. They say it reflects a new generation stepping forward to serve, one motivated by patriotism, opportunity and a willingness to answer the call.

A 14-year-old Montana rancher-in-training says God put him in the right place at the right time after he used the cowboy skills he'd spent months practicing to lasso and rescue a drowning man from the Yellowstone River following a rafting accident.
Jory Thomas was camping with his family near Greycliff, Montana, on July 5 when they heard someone screaming for help.
"We all heard, 'Help, help,'" Thomas told KTVQ. "There's two or three people floating down the river, one hanging on to the cooler, and he wasn't saying anything."
CALIFORNIA LIFEGUARD SPEAKS OUT ON HEARTSTOPPING OCEAN RESCUE: 'I LOVE WHAT I DO'
The Sweet Grass County Sheriff's Office honored Thomas with a Certificate of Achievement. (Facebook/Sweet Grass County Sheriff's Office)
A raft and paddleboard had struck a bridge pillar, throwing four people into the river. Three reached shore, but one man continued drifting downstream while clinging to a cooler.
Thomas said there was no time to wait.

"This current was pretty fast then, and he was moving pretty quickly," he said. "Only thing I could focus on was helping him get out of the water because I didn't want to see anyone go in front of me."
A general view of the Yellowstone River and the Absaroka Mountains on July 31, 2023, in Paradise Valley near Pray, Montana. (David Madison / Getty Images)

He emptied his pockets, crossed a waist-deep side channel and ran along the bank. Then he grabbed a 12-foot lariat he'd brought from home — something his grandmother told the station he'd never packed for a camping trip before.
"My first instinct, I thought, was try and rope him and drag him out before he gets too far down the river," Thomas said. "Luckily, I caught him first try."
The Yellowstone River erodes river banks as it flows north towards Livingston, Montana, on June 15, 2022. (Louise Johns for The Washington Post via Getty Images)
Thomas pulled the man toward shore through chest-deep water until first responders arrived.

The teenager said he'd only started taking roping seriously this year while helping with cattle on the family ranch, telling the station that his skills improving the more he roped cattle.
Thomas said he believes his faith guided him to act.
"God was basically putting me in the place of all this," he said. "God was just telling me all of this at the time and saying, 'Go get him, you got it, and I believe in you.'"
He later reflected that he never expected the same skills he learned on the ranch would save a person's life.
"I just thought I could help with cattle," Thomas said. "Not really helping humans and stuff like that. But I'm glad I was here to help."

title: Nancy Guthrie ransom notes release follows Unabomber ‘precedent' that cracked case, expert says
summary: A retired investigator says the release of ransom notes in the Nancy Guthrie kidnapping mirrors the 1995 strategy that helped identify the Unabomber.
story: Retired FBI agent Jason Pack exposes critical errors in the Pima County Sheriff's Department's investigation into the disappearance of Nancy Guthrie. title: Charlotte repeat offender charged with killing man hours after release on bond
summary: David Simpson allegedly shot two men in Charlotte less than two hours after his bond release from Mecklenburg County Jail on an unrelated charge.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A convicted killer allegedly shot two men, killing one, less than two hours after he was released from a North Carolina jail on bond last week, a stunning timeline that is raising fresh questions about why the repeat violent offender was free in the first place.

David Simpson, 29, is charged with first-degree murder, attempted first-degree murder, assault with a deadly weapon with intent to kill inflicting serious injury, and possession of a firearm by a felon in the July 29 shooting at an east Charlotte apartment complex. A Mecklenburg County judge on Friday ordered that he be held without bond.

Court records obtained by WCNC show Simpson was released from the Mecklenburg County Jail at 12:20 a.m. after posting a $10,000 bond on an unrelated charge of possession of a weapon by a prisoner. Police said the shooting happened less than two hours later, around 1:45 a.m., leaving one man dead and another seriously wounded.
HOUSE DEMOCRAT BLASTED AFTER EARLY RELEASE LAW FREED INMATES LATER CHARGED WITH MURDER

David Simpson, 29, is charged with first-degree murder, attempted first-degree murder, assault with a deadly weapon with intent to kill inflicting serious injury, and possession of a firearm by a felon in connection with the shooting. (Mecklenburg County Jail)

Police said the shooting followed a long-running dispute over a parking space outside the apartment complex. Officers had already been called to the property twice that night after arguments broke out between the victims and residents over where they had parked.

Surveillance video cited in the documents appears to show Simpson outside with his girlfriend when the victims' SUV drove past. Detectives said Simpson went inside, returned carrying what they described as a weighted black bag, and ran toward the victims.

Simpson was released from the Mecklenburg County Jail at 12:20 a.m. after posting a $10,000 bond on an unrelated charge of possession of a weapon by a prisoner, according to jail records. (Mecklenburg County Jail)

About 10 minutes later, two gunshots can be heard on the video. Roughly 30 seconds after that, Simpson is seen jogging back toward his apartment while handling the bag before driving away, investigators said. Officers recovered two spent 7.62-caliber rifle casings at the scene.
CRAZY BRAWL OVER A PARKING SPOT IN NEW YORK INCLUDES A VICIOUS SKATEBOARD TO THE HEAD
One victim died at the scene. The second made it inside an apartment before collapsing and later underwent surgery.

Court records show Simpson was previously charged with first-degree murder in a 2013 fatal shooting but pleaded guilty to voluntary manslaughter in 2015, Queen City News reported. He served about five years in prison before being released on parole in 2020.
Since then, he has been arrested several more times, including on multiple charges of possession of a firearm by a felon, WBTV reported.
DEMOCRATIC BOSTON COUNCILOR RIPS 'SOFT-ON-CRIME' POLICIES AFTER SUSPECTED GUNMAN'S VIOLENT PAST REVEALED
He also had pending charges this year for possession of a firearm by a felon, resisting a public officer and misdemeanor larceny, WCNC reported, citing court records.
Charlotte defense attorney Tim Cannady, who is not involved in the case, questioned why Simpson remained free despite his history.

"If you look at his history, it seems like this gentleman has picked up just about every year up to this point some kind of a violent crime," Cannady told WCNC. "So you kind of have to ask the question: Why wasn't he already in jail?"
An aerial view of the skyline of downtown Charlotte, North Carolina, on Oct. 12, 2023. (Omar Vega/Getty Images)
Former Charlotte City Council member Tariq Bokhari offered a similar criticism.

"We know what these top 1% of repeat offenders are going to do, and for some reason, we just don't have the appetite to take action," Bokhari told WBTV. "It feels like 'Groundhog Day,' to be quite honest."
Simpson refused to leave his jail cell for his first scheduled court appearance Friday morning, delaying the hearing until a judge ordered him to appear later that afternoon.

His girlfriend, Shakema Scott, has also been charged with accessory after the fact.
Simpson is due back in court on Aug. 21.

title: Idaho In-N-Out Burger shooting motive still a mystery as armed citizen speaks out
summary: An armed citizen and off-duty trooper returned fire at the Twin Falls In-N-Out Burger gunman, who was reportedly shocked by the armed response.
story: Twin Falls Police Chief Matthew Hicks identified 24-year-old Chad Williams as the suspect and said he died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound. Police warned that social media posts naming another man were

Police are still working to determine why a 24-year-old gunman opened fire at a crowded In-N-Out Burger in Twin Falls, Idaho, killing three people and wounding seven others before taking his own life after taking fire from a bystander and an off-duty Idaho state trooper.

Twin Falls Police Chief Matthew Hicks said Sunday that investigators were confident Chad Williams acted alone in Saturday's attack, but detectives had not yet established a motive or fully traced his movements before the shooting.

"We believe their actions helped drive the suspect away from the scene, preventing further casualties," Hicks said of an armed citizen and officer who returned fire. "We want to take a moment and commend the actions of the off-duty officer and the citizen, and their heroic action to stop this incident."

Police have not publicly identified the trooper or the bystander, but the Idaho Statesman detailed the heroics of Jordan Salinas, 35, of Kimberly, Idaho, strapped by the shoulder with a FN Five-seveN semi-automatic pistol fitted with a suppressor.
OFF-DUTY TROOPER AND ARMED CITIZEN HAILED AS HEROES AFTER RETURNING FIRE ON IN-N-OUT GUNMAN
This still image captured from video by a witness shows the scene of a shooting that started at an In-N-Out Burger restaurant Saturday, Aug. 1, 2026, in Twin Falls, Idaho. (Kevin Bell Jr. via AP)

Salinas, a reported "healthcare worker, the full-time caregiver of his wheelchair-bound brother," told the paper he took up gun training after a 2021 shooting – never even aiming a gun at an animal – saying he was able to "observe," "orient" and "decide" that "OK, this is the guy," he said before being resolute to "act."
The gunman, he said, was shocked by the armed response.
"He did not like it when bullets started firing both ways," Salinas, whose girlfriend at the restaurant was stuck in Williams fire, told the Statesman, adding he felt "no fear."
"There’s a task that needs to be done, and we’re the ones who need to do it," he added, only standing down when he said police took over the scene, thinking, "OK, my part is done."
The shooter was found dead from a self-inflicted gunshot wound near the restaurant, according to police.
MULTIPLE PEOPLE KILLED IN SHOOTING AT IDAHO IN-N-OUT RESTAURANT, SUSPECT DEAD
"These people are true heroes in our community," Twin Falls County Sheriff Jack Johnson said. "They diverted the shooter and without a doubt saved many lives."
Hicks said Williams' family was cooperating with authorities. Detectives were examining his activities before the shooting and trying to determine whether any victims had been deliberately targeted.
Authorities said seven people were injured. Two remained in critical condition Sunday, three were listed as stable and two had been treated and released from a hospital.
Officials said both fired at Williams during what authorities described as a chaotic and fast-moving attack, diverting his attention from the restaurant as customers and employees fled.
IN-N-OUT PRESIDENT SAYS ‘HEART IS BROKEN’ AFTER EMPLOYEE, CUSTOMERS KILLED IN IDAHO SHOOTING
This image provided by KMVT shows the scene of a shooting that started at an In-N-Out Burger restaurant, Saturday, Aug. 1, 2026 in Twin Falls, Idaho. (KMVT via AP)

Witness Lane Koehn, 34, said he was stopped at a traffic light near the restaurant when he saw a man carrying an AR-style rifle emerge from the drive-thru. Another man armed with a handgun then began firing at the shooter, Koehn told The Associated Press.
Koehn said he later saw an In-N-Out employee drag a wounded co-worker across the parking lot. The injured worker had been shot in the chest, he said.
"She was pretty bad off, but I don’t know. I hope she made it," Koehn said.
One of the three people killed was an In-N-Out employee, company owner Lynsi Snyder confirmed in a statement. Officials had not released the victims’ identities as they worked to notify relatives.
"My heart is broken, my chest is heavy, my eyes burn from the tears I’ve shed," Snyder said. "We lost one of our beautiful associates tonight."
"In-N-Out will be mourning with the families and praying for them as they tread through a very painful season."
Snyder said the employee had been caring for customers when she was killed. The company was working with police and offering support to victims, employees and their families.
The shooting erupted Saturday afternoon at the recently opened restaurant in a busy commercial area where hundreds of shoppers, diners and employees were believed to have been present.
Twin Falls resident Haley Dodaro said she and her mother were waiting in the drive-thru when they saw workers running from the restaurant and people fleeing across the road.
"At first," Dodaro said, she thought there might have been a fire. A person directing traffic then warned them that there was an active shooter.
"People were running out crying and screaming," she said. "It was very scary."

Nayeli Rodriguez, who was inside the restaurant with her daughters, said an employee told customers to get down after gunfire was heard near the kitchen. An older man tried to shield Rodriguez and her children before they escaped.
"We were trying to get as far as we could, and some angels let us in their car," Rodriguez said.

A local taxi company said one of its drivers, Terry Dudley, was shot twice in the back while charging his Tesla near the restaurant. North Star Taxi said Dudley survived but faced "a very long road ahead."
Salinas posted a humble Facebook message urging focus on "victims, their families, and everyone affected."

"The last 24 hours have been overwhelming," the message posted late Sunday night read. "I want to sincerely thank my family, friends, and everyone who has reached out with messages, prayers, and support. I haven't been able to respond to everyone yet, but please know I've seen your messages, and they mean more to me than I can put into words.
"In the coming days, I'll share a more complete account of what happened, to the best of my recollection, when I'm able.

"For now, my heart remains with the victims, their families, and everyone affected by yesterday's tragedy. Thank you for continuing to keep them in your thoughts and prayers, and thank you all for the incredible support you've shown me and my family."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The FBI asked members of the public to submit photographs and video recorded during the attack. Twin Falls police also urged anyone who witnessed the shooting or had relevant information to contact investigators.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Attorney who defended DC sniper says Kohberger faces 'monumental uphill battle' undoing guilty plea
summary: A criminal defense attorney explains why Bryan Kohberger's effort to undo his University of Idaho murders guilty plea faces two significant legal hurdles.
story: Bryan Kohberger, accused in the quadruple murder of University of Idaho students, is attempting to withdraw his previous guilty plea. Kohberger's post-conviction petition alleges ineffective assistance of counsel, coercion, disinformation, and false promises, seeking a new trial. Victims' families, including Kaylee Goncalves' mother, expressed disappointment but noted they were not surprised by this latest legal maneuver.

Bryan Kohberger faces a "monumental uphill battle" in his effort to withdraw his guilty plea in the murders of four University of Idaho students, according to an attorney who represented D.C. sniper Lee Boyd Malvo and once helped another client successfully withdraw a guilty plea before winning an acquittal.

Mark Petrovich, who represented Malvo in post-conviction proceedings in Virginia and has decades of criminal defense experience, told Fox News Digital that defendants rarely succeed in withdrawing guilty pleas after sentencing, even in cases involving claims that they were unaware of potentially exculpatory evidence before entering the plea.

He cautioned against drawing direct comparisons between Malvo's post-conviction litigation and Kohberger's effort to withdraw his guilty plea. Malvo's appeals stemmed from changes in constitutional law governing juvenile sentencing, while Kohberger is attempting to undo a plea agreement he entered as an adult after avoiding the death penalty.
KAYLEE GONCALVES' MOTHER SAYS FAMILY READY FOR TRIAL AFTER BRYAN KOHBERGER SEEKS TO WITHDRAW GUILTY PLEA

"It's a monumental uphill battle," Petrovich said. "First of all, getting the judge to allow you to withdraw the plea, and then second of all to winning any new proceeding, because there's a lot against you."

Bryan Kohberger appears at the Ada County Courthouse for his sentencing hearing on July 23, 2025, in Boise, Idaho. Kohberger pleaded guilty in exchange for being spared the death penalty for the stabbing of four University of Idaho students nearly three years ago. (Kyle Green-Pool/Getty Images)

Kohberger pleaded guilty in July 2025 to the stabbing deaths of University of Idaho students Ethan Chapin, Xana Kernodle, Madison Mogen and Kaylee Goncalves in Moscow, Idaho, in November 2022. He was sentenced to four consecutive life sentences without the possibility of parole after accepting a plea agreement that spared him from the death penalty.
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

In recent court filings, Kohberger claimed he was pressured into accepting the plea agreement, did not fully understand potentially exculpatory evidence before pleading guilty and was misled about the conditions he would face while incarcerated.
IDAHO MURDERS: NEW BOOK ON KOHBERGER REVEALS PREVIOUSLY UNSEEN EVIDENCE, CLAIMS SHEATH COULD BE INADMISSIBLE
He contends those factors undermined the voluntariness of his decision to plead guilty.

Petrovich said he once represented a client who sought to withdraw a guilty plea before sentencing. A judge granted the request, the case proceeded to trial and the client was acquitted, but he said Kohberger's circumstances are fundamentally different because he has already been sentenced.
In this Oct. 20, 2003 file photo, Lee Boyd Malvo listens to court proceedings during the trial of fellow sniper suspect John Allen Muhammad in Virginia Beach, Va.
SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS
"You can't wait until after you're sentenced and see what the consequences of the plea are and then change your plea," Petrovich said. "It's going to be a very, very difficult burden to overcome."
ALEX MURDAUGH MURDER SAGA LANDS RIGHT BACK WHERE IT STARTED BEFORE NEXT LOWCOUNTRY COURTROOM BATTLE
Petrovich said Kohberger would face two significant hurdles even if a judge allowed him to withdraw his plea.
One would be convincing jurors after previously admitting guilt under oath.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE
Even if a judge allowed Kohberger to withdraw his plea, Petrovich said jurors would almost certainly learn he had already admitted guilt, creating another significant obstacle at trial.
Bryan Kohberger attends a status hearing at Latah County District Court in Moscow, Idaho, U.S., January 12, 2023. (Kai Eiselein/Pool via REUTERS)
SEND US A TIP

"One thing that's important is that you still can't hide from the jury the fact that you said under oath that you're guilty," Petrovich said. "Even if you withdraw, then you have to explain that ... if you're going to get anywhere with any kind of jury finding."
Petrovich also questioned whether Kohberger's attorneys would have advised him to accept a plea agreement without first reviewing the evidence disclosed during discovery.
GOT A TIP?
He noted that defense attorneys handling capital cases typically spend years reviewing discovery before recommending whether a client should plead guilty.

"The attorneys on the case ... were intimately familiar with the evidence and the information that was provided to them by law enforcement and prosecution," Petrovich said. "I'm sure they knew all about everything. If they encouraged him or if there was a discussion and a plea was decided on, I'm sure it was for good reason."
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST
Kohberger's case is not the first involving a notorious killer who later sought to undo a guilty plea.

Madison Mogen, top left, smiles on the shoulders of her best friend, Kaylee Goncalves, as they pose with Ethan Chapin, Xana Kernodle, and two other housemates in Goncalves' final Instagram post, shared the day before the four students were stabbed to death. (@kayleegoncalves/Instagram)

James Earl Ray pleaded guilty in 1969 to assassinating the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. to avoid a potential death sentence. Three days after entering his guilty plea, Ray sought to withdraw it, arguing he had been pressured into confessing. He spent the rest of his life trying to undo the plea but died in prison in 1998 without ever receiving the jury trial he sought.
GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL

Serial killer Clifton Bloomfield unsuccessfully sought to withdraw guilty pleas after admitting to five murders in New Mexico to avoid capital punishment. Washington serial killer Robert Lee Yates Jr. also challenged his plea agreement after admitting to murdering 13 women, but courts ultimately rejected both efforts.

Kohberger's plea agreement spared him from facing a capital trial and ended years of pretrial litigation in one of the country's most closely watched murder prosecutions.
Petrovich said that history, combined with the years of discovery and plea negotiations leading up to Kohberger's agreement, makes the effort to withdraw it especially difficult.

title: Lindsay Clancy jurors visit crime scene in Karen Read-style move to test timeline: Retired judge

story: Psychiatrist Dr. Sejal Shah testified that Lindsay Clancy appeared honest and was not exaggerating psychiatric symptoms for legal gain.
This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, contact the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline at 988 or 1-800-273-TALK (8255).

Jurors in Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial retraced her ex-husband’s route Friday before walking through the Massachusetts home where the couple’s three children were killed, a court-supervised visit a retired Massachusetts judge said could help the panel understand the timeline and setting at the center of the case.
The move was reminiscent of another high-profile Massachusetts murder trial that recently captured headlines, when Karen Read was acquitted of the top charge during her 2025 retrial.
LINDSAY CLANCY’S EX-HUSBAND DETAILS ‘BIG SPIRAL’ AS EXPERT SAYS ONE PART ‘SCARED ME’ IN MOM’S MURDER TRIAL
Lindsay Clancy reacts as doctors testify about efforts to save her children Friday, July 31, 2026. (Josh Reynolds for Daily Mail /Pool)

In Clancy's case, the 18-member jury panel was driven past ThreeV restaurant in Plymouth and the CVS pharmacy in Kingston that Patrick Clancy visited on Jan. 24, 2023. Jurors were then escorted in groups of six through the family’s former home in Duxbury during a roughly 40-minute visit.

They also saw the basement where Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months, were found, as well as the yard beneath the second-story window where Lindsay Clancy was discovered seriously injured after attempting suicide. The fall left the woman paralyzed and in a wheelchair.

Jack Lu, who served 16 years as a Massachusetts Superior Court judge and five years as a Boston Municipal Court judge, said that, in his experience, a view is expected in a Massachusetts homicide trial, particularly a case involving multiple deaths.

"The reality is, on a homicide case, they’re always, always going to do a view," Lu, now a Boston College law professor, told Fox News Digital.

Karen Read exits the Norfolk County Superior Court, Friday, June 13, 2025, in Dedham, Mass. Read was acquitted of the top charge in her murder trial after being charged with killing her Boston police officer boyfriend by intentionally driving her SUV into him. (Richard Beetham for Fox News Digital)

Lu said the clearest benefit may be helping jurors assess how long Patrick was away from the home and understand the locations discussed throughout testimony.

"They’re going to dissect the amount of time involved in the husband’s trip to CVS," Lu said, adding that the visit could help jurors understand "what kind of time that Ms. Clancy had" after Patrick left.

Still, Lu cautioned against assuming the view necessarily favored either side or would become decisive.
KAREN READ SAYS SHE GETS FREE MEALS AND DISCOUNTS EVERYWHERE AFTER NOT GUILTY VERDICT
"The view is perhaps not obviously crucial to this case," he said. "It gives them context."

title: Deadliest animal in every US state revealed, from moose and bears to dogs
summary: A new report identifies the deadliest animal in every U.S. state, with snakes leading nationwide while bears, sharks, insects and even dogs top other regions.
story: Chaos survived after his owner shot a black bear that mauled him during a recent mushroom-foraging trip. (Credit: LORI PRICE/Fish Em LLC)
A demographic data platform has released a new report identifying the animals most likely to kill people in each U.S. state.
The 2026 report from World Population Review revealed a surprising mix of creatures topping the list, from large mammals such as moose to unexpected threats such as dogs and jellyfish.
According to the report, snakes make up the single largest category nationwide, with several species of rattlesnakes topping the list in multiple regions.
Georgia residents should be most cautious of the pygmy rattlesnake, while Oklahoma's biggest snake threat is the western pygmy rattlesnake.
CALIFORNIA TODDLER BITTEN BY RATTLESNAKE HIDING BENEATH AMAZON PACKAGE AMID ACTIVE SNAKE SEASON
Residents in Colorado, Maine, New Hampshire and Vermont should be cautious of moose. (Getty Images Creatives)
Meanwhile, Timber rattlesnakes claimed the top spot in both Connecticut and Kansas.
Southern Pacific rattlesnakes pose the biggest threat in California, while Arizona's deadliest species is the western diamondback rattlesnake.
Other rattlesnakes dominating state hazards include the prairie rattlesnake in North Dakota, the Mojave rattlesnake in Nevada and the eastern massasauga in Michigan.
Several non-rattlesnake species also rank as the deadliest animals in their respective states.
Louisiana's top threat is the eastern diamondback rattlesnake and Mississippi's is the cottonmouth snake.
Similarly, Indiana leads with the eastern copperhead, South Carolina points to the southern copperhead, and Hawaii stands out with the yellow-bellied sea snake as its primary concern.
NO CURE, NO VACCINE: EXPERTS WARN OF RARE BOURBON VIRUS AFTER FIRST NY CASE
Dogs pose the biggest threat to residents living in Alaska. (Getty Images)
Beyond reptiles, several states face risks from insects and other venomous creatures.
Wasps top the list in Iowa, ticks take the lead in Missouri, mosquitoes pose the highest danger in New York, and black widow spiders are the main concern in Alabama and Nebraska.
A handful of states should be cautious around coastal waters, according to the report.
Tiger sharks rank as the deadliest animal in Rhode Island, while bull sharks pose the greatest threat in Maryland and Virginia.

A jellyfish-like marine creature, called the Portuguese man o' war, is listed as the biggest danger in Delaware and North Carolina. Experts say that while its sting can be deadly in rare cases, it more commonly causes painful welts and skin irritation.
Alligators also rank as the deadliest animal in Florida and Texas, with the American alligator specifically topping Florida's list.
Large mammals also appear prominently throughout the report, with black bears ranking as the deadliest animals in Tennessee and Wisconsin.
North American black bears pose the greatest threat in Oregon, while American black bears top the list in Kentucky and Massachusetts.
In contrast, New Mexico's deadliest animal is the mountain lion, while moose are listed as the greatest risk in Colorado, Maine, New Hampshire and Vermont.
Grizzly bears also top the list in Idaho, Montana and Washington, and bison pose the greatest danger in South Dakota and Wyoming.
Whitetail deer were also identified as the deadliest animals in Arkansas, Ohio, West Virginia and Pennsylvania.
Alligators top the list as the deadliest animal for Floridians and Texans. (Getty Images)
In Alaska, despite commonly being household pets, dogs are listed as the state's most concerning animal.
Similarly, coyotes rank as the biggest threat in Illinois, Minnesota, New Jersey and Utah.

Overall, snakes dominate the threat landscape, topping the list in 14 states, according to the report.
Bears threaten eight states, while deer and other large ungulates account for 10 states.
Canines, including dogs and coyotes, rank as the deadliest animals in five states.
Biting and stinging arthropods, such as wasps, mosquitos and spiders, account for five states.
Equally, marine hazards also account for five states.

title: Spencer Pratt reacts to Spokane devastation with blunt wildfire warning and message of faith
summary: Spencer Pratt urges families not to wait for disaster after Spokane wildfire evacuation displaces thousands, drawing on his Palisades Fire experience.
story: Wildfires rip through Spokane County, Washington, forcing thousands of residents to evacuate as dry, windy conditions fuel multiple aggressive blazes. Gov. Jay Inslee declares a state of emergency while the National Guard deploys to assist local firefighters. Fire scientist Joaquin Ramirez joins to analyze the extreme weather outlook causing critical fire dangers across the Northwest.

As crews battle fast-moving wildfires that have destroyed hundreds of structures and forced thousands to evacuate in the Spokane area, one wildfire survivor is urging Americans to prepare before disaster strikes.

Former Los Angeles mayoral candidate and reality personality Spencer Pratt, whose Pacific Palisades home was destroyed in the 2025 Palisades Fire, said the devastation unfolding in Spokane is a warning for communities across the country.
"My deepest sympathies to the folks in Spokane who just lost everything in an instant," Pratt wrote in a lengthy social media post Sunday. "Nothing can really prepare you for this devastation."
Pratt, who has been outspoken about the emotional and financial toll of losing his own home, warned that communities across the country should not assume they are immune from similar disasters.
PALISADES FIRE SUSPECT ALLEGEDLY DRIVEN BY 'SOCIETAL REVENGE,' BEHAVIORAL ANALYST TESTIFIES IN COURT

Former reality television star Spencer Pratt, who lost his home in the Palisades fire, has been an outspoken critic of California leaders over their management of the wildfire recovery efforts. (MEGA/GC Images)
"And everyone else, take heed... this is coming for you, too," he wrote. "Don't wait til the fire is at your patio door."
He urged families to have an evacuation plan in place before disaster strikes, cautioning that wildfires often spread too quickly to leave time for last-minute decisions.
WOULD THIS SURVIVAL POD MAKE YOU FEEL SAFER?

"Have a plan. Don't expect government to be there to save your home," Pratt wrote. "Don't expect the fire to wait until you're at home and awake and ready... think about what happens when the fire comes at 2AM dead asleep, or when you're at work downtown, or 3 beers in on a river float 20 miles from home and your cats are all locked inside. You seldom get a real warning before the fire comes."
Pratt also reflected on the heartbreaking losses families face beyond their homes.
"As of now, I've not seen any reports of fatalities, thank God, and I pray there were none, but a lot of beloved pets undoubtedly perished, and for many, that's like losing family," he wrote.
EXCLUSIVE: WOMAN WHO STOLE $1.7M MEANT FOR HURRICANE VICTIMS GETS PRISON TIME AS DHS CRACKS DOWN ON FEMA FRAUD
The charred remains of a home destroyed by the Palisades Fire is seen in the Pacific Palisades neighborhood of Los Angeles, on January 13, 2025. (PATRICK T. FALLON/AFP via Getty Images)
He encouraged neighbors to support one another through what he predicted would be a lengthy recovery.
"Please look after your neighbors; they have a very long and painful road ahead, and everyone will move on from caring about Spokane in a week or so," Pratt wrote.
Pratt concluded his message by encouraging those affected to lean on their faith.

"Above all else, if I can offer any advice right now... lean further into God," he wrote. "The Lord is close to the brokenhearted and saves those who are crushed in spirit. Have faith in His providence, even if your heart feels too broken to accept it right now."

Amid the devastation, former Washington state Rep. Matt Shea shared a photo of an American flag still standing after flames swept through a neighborhood, calling it "an amazing picture of hope among the ashes."
"Some friends of ours lost everything... but Old Glory still survives," Shea wrote on X. "What an amazing picture of hope among the ashes. Thank you all for praying for us."
Former Seattle Seahawks quarterback Russell Wilson also shared a message of support on X, writing, "Praying for Spokane!"
As messages of support poured in, firefighters continued battling three major blazes being managed as part of the Spokane-area wildfire response.

According to Incident Commander Benjamin Cossel with the U.S. Department of Agriculture, the Autumn Lane Fire has burned 3,333 acres, the Old Trail Fire has scorched 3,481 acres, and the Fairview Fire has grown to 914 acres. All three fires remained 0% contained as of the latest update.
More than 900 firefighters and support personnel have been deployed across the three fires, with the Autumn Lane Fire remaining the primary focus.
An otherworldly scene in Spokane, Washington, as wildfires rage on Aug. 2, 2026. (South Pend Oreille Fire Rescue)

Authorities said approximately 5,000 homes have been evacuated as firefighters continue battling the blazes. Incident command has confirmed more than 600 structures have been destroyed, though officials cautioned that number could rise as crews gain access to damaged areas.
The American Red Cross Northwest Region said more than 400 people and their pets spent Saturday night at an emergency shelter in Spokane after the fast-moving wildfires forced widespread evacuations.
Firefighters respond to wildfire near Spokane, Washington, on Aug. 2, 2026. (South Pend Oreille Fire Rescue / FOX Weather)

"Extreme weather conditions led three separate wildfires to wreak havoc on Saturday, forcing widespread evacuations, causing extensive destruction, and forever changing the lives of those affected," the Red Cross said, adding that it has launched a "massive relief effort" and is seeking donations and volunteers to assist displaced residents.
Rep. Michael Baumgartner, R-Wash., said he spoke with Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin about the fire situation and potential federal assistance.

"After Gov. Ferguson requests emergency assistance he will take the official request for FEMA support to President Trump," Baumgartner wrote on X, adding that he appreciated Mullin's "care and concern for what our community is experiencing."
Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson later said he spoke directly with President Donald Trump and Mullin, describing the devastation unfolding in Spokane and elsewhere across the state.
"Just a few minutes ago, I spoke with President Trump and Secretary Mullin. I detailed how dire and devastating the situation is in Spokane and across our state," Ferguson wrote on X.
Ferguson said Trump "expressed his concern for the people of Washington during this difficult time" and that the two would "be working together on additional requests for federal assistance."
"I deeply appreciate the President taking time to have this conversation, and I am optimistic we will receive a quick approval for our request for a federal emergency declaration," Ferguson wrote.
Sen. Patty Murray, D-Wash., said she also spoke with Mullin and said the federal government is closely tracking the disaster.
"He made clear the federal government will do everything it can to support response and recovery—that is my top priority right now and I deeply appreciate that commitment," Murray wrote on X.
Calling the destruction "heartbreaking," Murray said "it will be a long road to recovery."

"Right now, EVERYONE needs to listen carefully to local officials," she wrote. "I am so grateful to our fire crews and first responders who are saving lives, including our WA National Guard, servicemembers from Fairchild, and the many individuals coming from out of state to fight these fires."

Heavy smoke blankets the Spokane area as firefighters battle several fast-moving wildfires that have forced thousands of evacuations and prompted a massive emergency response. (Spokane Valley Fire Department)

As the response continued, the Spokane County Board of Commissioners unanimously declared a state of emergency, giving county officials additional authority to quickly purchase emergency equipment and supplies.

"My heart goes out to those who have been affected by these devastating fires and my prayers are with the first responders who will continue working through the night and into tomorrow," Spokane County Commissioner Mary Brooks said.
Officials also urged people to stay away from lakes, rivers and other waterways where firefighting aircraft are collecting water to battle the blazes.

Emergency officials warned boaters, kayakers, paddleboarders and others on the water to give aircraft plenty of space as they make frequent low-level passes, saying doing so is critical to keeping both crews and the public safe while allowing firefighters to continue protecting threatened communities.

title: Bryan Kohberger's former defense expert calls for death penalty, says investigators missed key evidence
summary: A defense expert hired by Bryan Kohberger now says cellphone data shows evidence of stalking, but prosecutors never introduced it ahead of the guilty plea.
story: A judge approved Bryan Kohberger's request for a new lawyer in his attempt to secure a new trial, despite his previous guilty plea for murdering four University of Idaho students in 2022. Legal analyst Mehek Cooke discusses the high bar for overturning a guilty plea, while the victim's family expresses the pain of reliving the tragedy.

Admitted Idaho murderer Bryan Kohberger should get a new trial and face the death penalty, according to a digital forensics expert hired by the defense who says investigators missed damning evidence against the 30-year-old former criminology PhD student — evidence he told Fox News Digital investigators never properly analyzed or incorporated into the prosecution's case.

Sy Ray is a former Arizona homicide investigator who is now an expert on digital forensics, geolocation and similar data. Kohberger's lawyers hired him as an expert witness for the defense before Kohberger pleaded guilty to avoid the death penalty for the home invasion murders of Kaylee Goncalves, 21, Madison Mogen, 21, Xana Kernodle, 20, and Ethan Chapin, also 20.

Kohberger, now serving four consecutive sentences of life in prison without parole, petitioned the court last week to withdraw his guilty plea and seek post-conviction relief, which could send the case to trial — and put the potential death penalty back in play.
KOHBERGER DEFENSE EXPERT WANTS HIS LAWYERS UNDER OATH AFTER KILLER CITES FINDINGS IN BID TO UNDO GUILTY PLEA
Families of Idaho murder victims file wrongful death lawsuit against Washington State University, alleging the school ignored 13 reports about Bryan Kohberger. (AP Photo/Kyle Green, Pool; Instagram)
"Bring back the death penalty," Ray told journalist Brian Entin in a new podcast. "I am all for this."

He said he is confident that Kohberger would be convicted and claimed that Kohberger's smartphone data is much more incriminating than was revealed previously when police and the courts unsealed thousands of pages of evidence in the case.

"I 100% believe that the offender, who is Bryan Kohberger — there’s no alternative theory in my head at this point," Ray said in the 82-minute episode, which also included Goncalves’ parents, Kristi and Steve, and her older sister, Alivea. "I 100% believe he’s been in the house before."
BRYAN KOHBERGER'S CHOICE OF 'A HOUSE FULL OF WOMEN' MAY HOLD THE KEY TO THE IDAHO MURDERS' BIGGEST MYSTERY
A watchman parked outside 1122 King Road on Dec. 11, 2022, four weeks after four students were stabbed to death inside. (Michael Ruiz/Fox News Digital)
Ray told Entin that the evidence he reviewed shows Kohberger potentially inside the victims’ home, or at least in proximity outside, and at other places when they were present prior to the murders.

He told Fox News Digital that he didn't have to address this evidence in his own expert report, filed by the defense in January 2025, because he based it only on the contents of the reports produced by prosecution experts, which left out something called a location database of record, or LOCDBOR report, that he alleges contains damning new information about Kohberger's movements in his semester at Washington State University.

Ray acknowledged that his January 2025 report appears different from his current public comments but said the report evaluated only the prosecution's work product, not the underlying AT&T records he says investigators never mapped.

"My summary of no evidence is based on that work product and the work product that the state had put together at that time," he told Fox News Digital.  "I can't put in my defense report, 'Hey, if you guys would just go look at the LOCDBOR report here, you'll solve your case and have a really rock solid case.' But I can put, here are some follow-up items that I would expect you guys to do. And one of those things is you'll see repeated over and over, you have to map all the data. Please go map all the data."

Speaking on the podcast, Ray said the LOCDBOR report contains location data that he believes shows Kohberger stalked the victims.  Fox News Digital has not independently reviewed the LOCDBOR report, either, as it is not among thousands of pages of unsealed court documents in the case.

"If you look at those precise measurements, there’s probably five that land directly on what would be the living room of the house," Ray told Entin. "Like the latitude-longitude is the physical house itself, and if you put the house back on the map, and you map those, the hits are inside the house."
IDAHO MURDERS: NEW BOOK ON KOHBERGER REVEALS PREVIOUSLY UNSEEN EVIDENCE, CLAIMS SHEATH COULD BE INADMISSIBLE

Kohberger pleaded guilty to avoid the death penalty for the home invasion murders of Kaylee Goncalves, Madison Mogen, Xana Kernodle and Ethan Chapin. (Instagram @xanakernodle / @maddiemogen / @kayleegoncalves)

"I just want to make sure I understand correctly… because I haven't heard this before — so you're saying, based on the data you saw, the latitude-longitude for Bryan Kohberger’s Samsung was in the living room?" Entin asked.

"The AT&T-derived latitude-longitude from the AT&T’s network that it estimates a location, it lands in the house — and it's a 25-meter range, so we're talking 75 feet, so it could be anywhere in the house on any floor," Ray said. "It could technically be outside the house, it could [be] on the property, but it's showing in the immediate area. My personal opinion is when I look at those, and I map what's happening before and after and I'm looking at all the other evidence. I think these are accurate locations."
Speaking with Fox News Digital, he said he couldn't be certain that Kohberger actually went inside, but the geolocation data is damning in other ways.

"What's really telling is there's times where he's in that area, and then you'll see one of the victim's phones move over to this little A&W place, and then his phone moves over," Ray told Fox News Digital. "And the idea that, you know, these are just total random and there's no accuracy to it — we're actually seeing phones tracked together."
SEND US A TIP

Ray said on the podcast that his theory is that Mogen was Kohberger’s primary target due to the number of times he could trace their phones to similar locations — but he noted later that Mogen was often with Goncalves, and their phones moved together a lot.
Madison Mogen, 21, was one of four University of Idaho students killed in a home invasion attack at their off-campus rental in November 2022. (Jessie Frost Photography)

"I believe Maddie was the target," he said, adding that repeated "collisions" between their phones placed them in roughly the same area at the same time, including at a Pullman party the first week of school and at the A&W store near the King Road crime scene.
He also flagged what he described as Kohberger’s broader "pattern of life," pointing to evidence of stalking before the murders.
Because the state's "work product" didn't use this data, he said, his report only pushed back on what the state's witnesses used, which he said is lacking and missed the phone "collisions" entirely.
GET REAL-TIME UPDATES DIRECTLY ON THE TRUE CRIME HUB

"I am unable to locate any period of time between June 23, 2022 and November 13, 2022 where Mr. Kohberger’s mobile device is in the same specific area as any of the deceased’s mobile devices," he wrote.
Bryan Christopher Kohberger is seen in a booking photo after his arrest on Dec. 30, 2022, in Pennsylvania. (Monroe County Correctional Facility via Getty Images)
That pattern of life was also broken on the night of the murders, when Ray said he believes the plan to target Mogen went awry and resulted in him fleeing south, where he’d never driven before.

While prosecutors alleged that Kohberger had visited the crime scene a dozen times before the murders and at least once the morning after, they have not pointed to "collisions" with any of the victims the way Ray described in the podcast. In a news briefing after Kohberger's guilty plea, the case's lead investigators said they didn't know who the target was.

"The evidence suggested that there was a reason that this particular house was chosen," said then-Moscow Police Cpl. Brett Payne. "What that reason is, we don't know. We don't know who the target was, and we're not going to speculate on that up here today. But we can tell you that, for whatever reason, Mr. Kohberger chose that residence. Perhaps it's the location, layout, we do not know."
And when they were asked by Fox News Digital if they had a motive, lead investigators replied, "We don't."

Cpl. Brett Payne of the Moscow Police Department, left, and Lt. Darren Gilbertson of the Idaho State Police speak to the media during a press conference at the Ada County Courthouse after the sentencing of Bryan Kohberger, July 23, 2025. (AP Photo/Kyle Green, Pool)
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X
Ray has maintained that investigators missed the evidence and should go back and take another look in case Kohberger's attempt to withdraw his plea and appeal his conviction succeeds.
"They need to get experts who actually know what the hell they’re looking at, and they need to rebuild the case now," he said.

Morgan Wright, another expert on digital forensics who is not connected to the case, said he is skeptical without seeing the LOCDBOR data firsthand.
"Show me the report. Show me the map," said Wright, the host of "Crime: Reconstructed" and the CEO and founder of the National Center for Open and Unsolved Cases. "Don't tell me, show me."
Wright, who has been following the case, said he hasn't seen LOCDBOR references in connection with the investigation prior to the podcast interview.
Ray argues the records speak for themselves if investigators are willing to revisit them.

After Kohberger’s guilty plea, Ray said he offered to do a debrief with the FBI to show the evidence he said he found and they missed. He said he got no response, but added that he has presented before hundreds of law enforcement agencies around the country going back to November, he said.
Idaho State Correctional Complex in Kuna, Idaho, where Bryan Kohberber is being housed, on July 22, 2025. (Derek Shook for Fox News Digital)
Last week, Kohberger filed a petition for post-conviction relief, claiming he had ineffective counsel from his defense team.
Ray also speculated that Kohberger’s post-conviction petition was part of a broader legal strategy by his lead defense attorney Anne Taylor despite the plea agreement’s waiver of most appeal rights.
Kohberger pleaded guilty to avoid the death penalty.
"This can never be the standard investigation that we see in cases," Ray said. "This can never be acceptable."
Bryan Kohberger sits with Anne Taylor, one of his attorneys, during a hearing in Latah County District Court, Sept. 13, 2023, in Moscow, Idaho. (AP Photo/Ted S. Warren, Pool)
However, he said he’s confident Kohberger would be convicted anyway at trial — if investigators introduced the evidence he found while working with Taylor.
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST
"The time is now to start this investigation over," Ray said.
Kohberger had followed other people in the Moscow-Pullman area, he said — a pair of college towns on the border of Washington and Idaho.
"I think he had multiple targets throughout the entire Moscow-Pullman area," Ray said. "Location information and pattern of life is by far the most telling."

Ray said he has no doubt that Kohberger committed the murders.
"If he ever does walk, he will kill again," he said.

title: Southern university requires business suits, bans du-rags and other headwear in new dress code
summary: Tuskegee University's new dress code bans du-rags, bonnets and sagging pants in classrooms as part of its broader workforce readiness push.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

Retired U.S. Air Force Maj. Gen. Dr. Mark Brown, president and CEO of Tuskegee University in Alabama, is bringing forward a "professional educational environment" to one of the nation's most prestigious Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCU).

Students will be required to bring a business suit and shoes to campus for business-like meetings and cannot dress unprofessionally in the classrooms or cafeterias. Head coverings will also be barred, with exceptions for those that serve religious or medical purposes.

"The university has developed a new policy for student attire on campus, classroom attendance, and cell phone use in classrooms," Brown wrote in a message to students. "Tuskegee students now have a dress code for public and professional places."

"The Student Handbook requires students to arrive on campus with a business suit and proper shoes for a business meeting," the message said. "Students are prohibited from wearing revealing clothing in class, to the cafeteria or in official settings like Convocation. They are also not able to wear bedroom shoes, bonnets, or du-rags to class or the cafeteria."
MICHELLE OBAMA ACCUSES MEDIA OF WEAPONIZING FASHION TO 'DIMINISH' HER AS A CAMPAIGN THREAT
Retired Maj. Gen. Mark Brown was commissioned through the ROTC program at Tuskegee University in Alabama, and entered active duty in 1986. (U.S. Air Force)
The Alabama school is also restricting revealing and sexually explicit clothing as part of a broader push to prepare college students for the workforce.

"The goal here is not meant to restrict you from enjoying the Tuskegee Experience, but to prepare you with a solid foundation for the workforce you will enter once you leave Tuskegee," Brown, who took over as Tuskegee University president two years ago, wrote. "Employers are less forgiving and too often presentation may overrule stellar preparation.

"Tuskegee University continues to prepare the best and brightest for a lifetime of success," Brown added. "With these changes, we want to ensure every student is as prepared as they can be. I look forward to seeing you in August."
STUDENT LOAN RULE WOULD PENALIZE GRADUATES WHO ENTER MINISTRY, CHRISTIAN COLLEGE LEADERS SAY

Tuskegee University in Alabama is one of the most prestigious Historically Black Colleges and Universities in America and a former U.S. Air Force major general is bringing some requirements of professionalism to the campus.

Tuskegee’s fall orientation guidance lists business attire for career fairs, meetings, interviews and other professional occasions, but the guidance does restrict unprofessional attire in classrooms, too.

"Hats, bonnets, head scarves, caps, hoods, du-rags, bandanas, sunglasses, and other non-religious or non-medically required head coverings should be removed while in the classroom or cafeteria unless they are required for documented medical, religious, cultural, or University-approved purposes," the Dress Code Policy for Students that accompanied Brown's message read.

"Pants, skirts, dresses, and shorts should be worn in a manner that is appropriate for a professional educational environment. Clothing should fit properly and not expose undergarments or other private areas. Excessively short shorts, swimsuit bottoms, body suits, sleeveless undershirts, and similar casual garments are not appropriate for professional classroom settings," the guidance continued. "T-shirts worn as dresses and sagging pants are not permitted. Baggy or loose fitting pants must be worn with a belt that fits around the waist."
UNITED PASSENGER SAYS CREW ORDERED HIM TO CHANGE CONTROVERSIAL T-SHIRT BEFORE HE COULD TRAVEL
Faculty members will be authorized to respond when students are dressed in violation of the guidelines, though the president’s message did not specify potential penalties.

Some elements of the announcement reinforce standards that were already on the books. Tuskegee’s 2025-26 student handbook required students to dress "in good taste," prohibited sleepwear outside residence halls and barred men from wearing "do rags," stocking caps, bandanas, baseball caps and other headwear inside university buildings. It also prohibited sagging pants in academic facilities.

The revised rules have fueled a wider debate over professionalism, cultural expression and the expectations placed on students at HBCUs. Critics online have described restrictions on du-rags and bonnets as respectability politics that unfairly target clothing associated with Black culture.
Supporters argue that colleges should teach students how to present themselves during interviews, meetings and other professional situations.

Several alumni have defended the university’s approach. Tuskegee graduate Gwen McKinney told NBC4 Washington that the policy was "a breath of fresh air," saying there is "a time and place and a setting for every kind of dress."
White Hall is a historic building at Tuskegee University in Alabama. (Carol M. Highsmith/Buyenlarge/Getty Images)

"A critical part of being ready for and confident in business environments is being appropriately dressed," Walter P. Cooper Sr., director of the Career Education and Leadership Development Center, said.

"We know that every workplace doesn’t require business attire – our center includes business casual and casual attire, too – but as our students prepare to enter those workplace scenarios that do, it is important that access to the right wardrobe is not a barrier."
For students that might not have the proper attire, there is The Golden Tigers Community Closet to help outfit needy students.

"One of the key pillars of Tuskegee’s Renaissance Era is our focus on career readiness for our students," Brown said. "Academically, we are equipping our students to stand shoulder to shoulder with any candidates competing for roles in the global economy.
"The Golden Tigers Community Closet is an important way to ensure that every student can also feel confidently dressed when they step into those spaces."

The dress code is part of a larger set of classroom and career-readiness rules being introduced as Tuskegee expects its highest new-student enrollment in 32 years. Cellphone use will be prohibited unless authorized by an instructor.
"Faculty will be empowered to respond to students who are inappropriately dressed based on these guidelines," Brown's message to students added.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Faculty will also be able to respond to a different classroom challenge – cell phones. Unless directed by the professor, students are no longer allowed to use their cell phones while in class. They should be turned off to eliminate any distraction from the instructor’s lesson."

Fox News Digital reached out to Brown's office and the university for further comment. VP of stragetic communications Thonnia Lee confirmed the details of the president's message to students and the dress code but declined further comment.

title: Florida ‘sadist’ charged after allegedly being hired by UK woman to torture and kill her
summary: A deleted video and Discord messages reveal a UK woman's final hours inside a Florida Airbnb before she was found in a shallow grave.
story: Internet searches from conman Brian Walshe and voicemails from his mother, Diana, take center stage in new Fox Nation special on the Ana Walshe murder case.
If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 1-800-273-TALK (8255).
WARNING: GRAPHIC CONTENT

A Florida man is behind bars awaiting trial after allegedly killing a young woman who traveled from the United Kingdom to pay him to carry out their plan for her to be "sexually abused, tortured, and murdered," court records show.
Sonia Exelby of Portsmouth, England, was reported missing in October 2025 by her family when she failed to return home from a trip to the United States, records show.
Text communications to one of Exelby’s friends suggest she’d regretted her decision and wanted to back out of the deal she’d allegedly made with Hall to torture and kill her, records show.
FLORIDA MAN WHO ALLEGEDLY LURED WOMEN WITH DATING APP COULD HAVE MORE VICTIMS: AUTHORITIES

Sonia Exelby of Portsmouth, England, right, was found in a shallow grave with stab wounds in Ocala, Florida. Dwain Hall, left, has been charged in her killing. (Marion County Sheriff's Office / Facebook)
But it apparently was too late.
Days later, investigators found her body in a shallow grave in a wooded area in Ocala, Florida.
Now 54-year-old Dwain Hall of Ocala, Florida, faces charges of premeditated, first-degree murder and kidnapping. His trial is scheduled for Nov. 5 in Marion County, Florida.
Hatching a deadly plan
In 2023, Hall and Exelby met on a "fetish website" where they discussed "bondage, suicide, and her desire to have someone kill her," according to court records.
Hall, a self-described sadist, allegedly started what he described as a process of "mentoring" Exelby, investigators who reviewed their messages said.
A Facebook page attributed to Hall shows a fascination with Anubis, said to be the Egyptian god of the underworld.
In the year leading up to her death, Exelby offered to "help Hall with money he owed to the IRS," their online conversation showed, according to investigators.

They allegedly agreed that Exelby would pay him $4,000 cash to pay his debt in exchange for his help achieving "what she wanted," court records show. And they allegedly came up with a "cover story," to tell their families, and potentially law enforcement, records show.
After two years of online messaging, the young woman with a love of singing booked a flight from England to a rural area of North Florida to meet Hall, investigators said.
It wasn’t the first time she’d hatched a plan for her death, reports show.

Authorities in the United Kingdom thwarted a 2024 attempt by Exelby to travel to meet "online individuals who would be willing to kill her violently," court records show. And she had "known mental health diagnoses," investigators said.

This time, court records show, Exelby left evidence on her computer indicating that she was "again suicidal and traveling to the United States to be possibly sexually abused, tortured, and murdered by unknown individuals living in the United States."
Exelby flew to Gainesville Regional Airport in Gainesville, Florida, on the evening of Oct. 10, 2025. She had a return flight scheduled for Oct. 13.
A deleted video and chilling Discord messages reveal a UK woman's final hours inside a Florida Airbnb before she was found in a shallow grave. (Sonia Exelby/Facebook)
Investigators said Hall picked up Exelby in a vehicle and took her to an Airbnb 40 minutes south in Reddick, Florida. She’d reserved it in her name, court records show.
Before picking her up at the airport, Hall purchased gun cleaner, 50 feet of rope, Lume spray deodorant, and sturdy, nylon, parachute cord at a Gainesville Walmart.
After paying for the items, he went back for one more thing—a shovel.
Those alleged details were gathered by investigators with the Florida Department of Law Enforcement, who reviewed Walmart receipts and surveillance video.
‘So scared’ and ‘So broken’
On Oct. 11, after spending one night with Hall, Exelby sent "long, and at times disjointed" messages to a friend through Discord, investigators said.

Exelby allegedly wrote that "last night was so bad," and Hall had her "locked in" and had taken her phone because "he doesn't trust me with it," records show. She noted there was poor cellphone signal "in the middle of nowhere."
She fretted about regret and a gruesome choice.
"I thought he'd do it quick and not give my mind time to stew," she wrote. She said she knew it would be her last communication "if I don't take his offer of shooting him," she wrote.
In the messages, she said the person she was with "made her record three disclaimer videos and write a letter to her family because he thought it was ‘funny,’" investigation notes show.
"I'm so so scared I'm so broken and in so much pain all I can do is lay here," Exelby wrote. "I'm sorry I don't even know what I'm saying and I'm trying to be quick and my time’s up."
Missing, then found
On Oct. 11, the same day Exelby messaged her friend, Hall’s bank account for his roadside assistance business charged Exelby's debit card seven times within about 10 minutes.
After Exelby didn’t show up for her Oct. 13 flight home, she was reported missing.
Shortly after, charges to Exelby’s debit card paid to Hall’s business helped lead investigators to him.

On Oct. 17, law enforcement found Exelby’s body buried in a shallow grave in a wooded area of Marion County, court records show. Four stab wounds were found on the side of her body. The label for the shovel Hall bought at Walmart was found in the top layers of dirt, investigators said.
That same day, Hall was spotted by sheriff’s deputies and was pulled over while driving his black Jeep Cherokee on Interstate 75 in the Ocala area.
Exelby's body was found in the Ocala, Florida, area. (Photo by Nick Conzone)
DATING-APP CHARMER ACCUSED OF MURDER AFTER HISTORY OF DOMESTIC ARRESTS INVOLVING WOMEN HE MET ONLINE

Before being taken into custody, investigators said Hall allegedly messaged a friend over Facebook about a package he was sending that contained "precious and valuable personal items." "Will need this back in 6 months if this storm passes over with no lingering fallout," Hall allegedly wrote in the messages reviewed by investigators. "Please for the love of shadows don't lose this box."
Investigators later recovered the package contents from Hall’s friend. They found a bracelet and a black, seven-inch, steel knife "designed for piercing and stabbing," court records show.

The knife blade was engraved with the words: "Dorkworf pointy end goes in the other guy." The friend told investigators that "Dorkworf" was "making fun of Hall's use of the Darkwolf name while online."
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X
DNA from blood samples recovered from the knife matched Exelby’s.
Initially, Hall denied to investigators that he knew Exelby, court records show.
But eventually, he described how he’d taken a video of her, but that she "was not behaving right so he deleted it."
Frightening video
Investigators later recovered the video that Hall recorded the same day Exelby messaged her friend. It had been deleted three seconds later, records show.

The 4-minute-and-16-second video shows a bruised, "disheveled" Exelby "sitting on a piece of furniture" in the Airbnb. Hall allegedly can be heard asking her questions and directing her answers, reports show. In the video, Exelby "rarely looks up towards the camera where Hall would be positioned, becomes visibly upset with tears in her eyes, exhales deeply, swallows hard, and is very hesitant to answer Hall's questions," investigators wrote in an affidavit.

When Hall asks Exelby to tell him "why she is here," she responds, "Because I'm an awful person."
When pressed by Hall, Exelby explains, "I've crushed everyone who ever loves me."

When pressed further to say how she "would want to die," Exelby hesitates, then says she wants to be stabbed.
Under his questioning, she reveals that she’s been beaten over the past days. When asked if she was coerced, she silently shakes her head.
SEND US A TIP
Hall demands, "This is how you wanted to die, right? You wanted to be beaten and made to suffer because you're such a piece of s---."
A Florida man faces a murder trial after allegedly killing a U.K. woman who went missing during a trip to meet him. Her body was found in a shallow grave in Ocala, Florida. (Sonia Exelby/Facebook)
She nods.

Hall orders: "Say it."
"I needed to be beaten and suffer cause I'm such a piece of s---," Exelby says.

"Good, good," Hall replies. He asks her if she is happy and getting what she wants.

She didn’t bring him cash and he was upset, he allegedly told them.

Instead, she gave him her debit card to charge. But he was only able to get $1,200 from it after it was declined several times. title: Moscow bombing exposes potential security gaps around Putin’s military elite, expert says
summary: An analyst warns Putin’s effort to project normalcy may have left Moscow exposed after a fatal restaurant bombing reportedly targeted a senior Russian general at a private celebration.
story: Fox News correspondent Stephanie Bennett reports on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirming a drone attack on Russia that killed three people on ‘Fox Report.’

Russian President Vladimir Putin's drive to project "normalcy" in Moscow may have created a dangerous security blind spot, giving adversaries like Ukraine greater opportunities to target the Kremlin's military elite, an analyst said Monday.

The assessment came after a deadly explosion ripped through an upscale Moscow restaurant on Aug. 1, where a senior Russian general was reportedly attending a private celebration. Several Russian media outlets claimed the bombing targeted Col. Gen. Alexander Chaiko, who led the troops that made a botched attempt to storm the Ukrainian capital in 2022 and recently was appointed the chief of Russia’s aerospace forces. The claims could not be independently verified.

If Chaiko was indeed at the restaurant, "that would establish a compelling motive for Ukraine," Dr. Mark Episkopos, a Eurasia research fellow at the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, told Fox News Digital. "But there has been an ongoing discourse inside Russia that, despite numerous such attacks, Russian elites and even military figures continue to flout [operational security] best practices by holding parties like this in the first place."

The Russian Embassy in Rome accused Kyiv of carrying out the attack and said in a statement Aug. 2 that the attack was "evidence that the Ukrainian terrorist contagion is already beginning to spread."
MAYOR CALLS UPSCALE RESTAURANT BOMBING A 'BRUTAL TERRORIST ACT'
Law enforcement officers and emergency services personnel stand near the site of an explosion at a restaurant in central Moscow, Russia, on Aug. 1, 2026. (REUTERS)

"The other factor here is that Putin has done his best to preserve a sense of ‘normalcy’ in Moscow and St. Petersburg, cultivating a facade of stability that Ukraine has been able to exploit," Episkopos added.

Russia’s National Anti-Terrorism Committee said an unidentified woman carried an improvised explosive device to the Balzi Rossi restaurant. The committee said the woman was stopped by security before the bomb was detonated near the restaurant's entrance. The Russian Embassy in Rome on Monday said five people were killed and 19 were injured in the attack.
UKRAINE LAUNCHES WHAT APPEARS TO BE ONE OF ITS LARGEST DRONE ATTACKS AGAINST RUSSIA: REPORT
Police block an area near a deadly explosion at a restaurant in Moscow, Saturday, Aug. 1, 2026. (Sergei Vedyashkin/Moscow News Agency via AP)
"This particular event did seem to have a substantial level of security, which is why the person carrying the explosive was reportedly stopped and questioned at the entrance," Episkopos noted.
Russian investigators suggested the courier may not have known she was transporting explosives and said the device was detonated remotely.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin condemned the "brutal terrorist attack," vowing that those responsible would be punished, according to Deutsche Welle.
'A NEW KIND OF WAR': INSIDE UKRAINE'S HIDDEN FACTORIES MASS-PRODUCING COMBAT DRONES
Russian President Vladimir Putin crosses himself during the Orthodox Easter service at the Cathedral of Christ the Saviour in Moscow on April 12, 2026. (Alexander Zemlianichenko/AP)

"The means by which this attack was executed — a remotely detonated explosive device delivered on-site by a civilian — are also consistent with other assassinations deep inside Russian territory previously attributed to Ukraine," Episkopos said.
"These include those of Lt. Gen. Igor Kirillov, Lt. Gen. Yaroslav Moskalik, Lt. Gen. Fanil Sarvarov, pro-Kremlin blogger Vladlen Tatarsky and others," he said.
Ukraine had not publicly commented on the restaurant bombing as of Monday afternoon, and no group had claimed responsibility.
Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Moscow has repeatedly accused Kyiv of targeting senior military officers, pro-war figures and Russian-installed officials.
MOSCOW, TALIBAN FORGE MILITARY ALLIANCE IN POWER GRAB AFTER US AFGHANISTAN EXIT: REPORTS
Smoke rises from a Russian tank destroyed by Ukrainian forces, on the side of a road in Lugansk region on February 26, 2022. (ANATOLII STEPANOV/AFP via Getty Images)
Episkopos noted that Kyiv has increasingly used unconventional tactics to offset Russia's superiority in conventional manpower and firepower.

"Ukraine has pioneered a new style of asymmetric warfare that plays to its strengths and Russia's weaknesses — relatively porous borders and vast territory that's difficult to monitor, let alone defend," he said. "Ukraine's interior is smaller and comparatively better controlled, and the intelligence it receives from Western partners plays a role here."
NATO MEMBER SCRAMBLES FIGHTER JETS AS RUSSIAN ATTACK ON UKRAINE KILLS 8

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky speaks at a press conference after meetings with the heads of the EU and Ireland, following a formal ceremony to mark the launch of Ireland's eighth EU presidency, at Dublin Castle in Dublin on July 1, 2026. (Paul Faith / AFP via Getty Images)
