title: Sudan's forgotten war leaves millions hungry as global attention remains elsewhere
summary: El Fasher and El Obeid remain flashpoints as UN reports detail war crimes, mass rape, and genocide conditions in Sudan's escalating civil war.
story: New footage shows families lining up for water as UNICEF warns children continue to bear the brunt of the war. (Video: UNICEF via AP.)
As multiple international crises grip the world, from Iran to Russia’s war in Ukraine, Sudan quietly remains one of the largest humanitarian and displacement disasters in the world.

Since the outbreak of hostilities in 2023, over 14 million people have been displaced and nearly 34 million people are in desperate need of humanitarian support, accounting for 10% of global needs, according to the International Rescue Committee.

"The war in Sudan has caused the world's largest humanitarian crisis and has escalated into a regional war involving all of its neighbors as well as numerous Middle Eastern powers," Alan Boswell, Project Director for the Horn of Africa at International Crisis Group, told Fox News Digital.
"Despite this, world leaders continue to ignore the conflict, leaving it to subordinates. That approach continues to fail," Boswell added.
COULD THIS AFRICAN NATION BECOME TRUMP'S NEXT TERROR TARGET AS JIHADISTS CLOSE IN ON POWER?

Women and children queue to receive free food being distributed in al-Mohayra camp for displaced people, near the city of El-Obeid in the southern Kordofan region, on June 29, 2026.  (AFP via Getty Images)
The United Nations says that some 19.5 million people are experiencing acute hunger, and 4.5 million people have fled the country.
The U.S. also recently imposed an additional round of sanctions against the Sudanese Armed Forces for allegedly using chemical weapons in 2024 in violations of the Chemical Weapons Convention.
The Sudanese government denied the allegations.

The Trump administration has made significant efforts in trying to mediate between Russia and Ukraine, as well as bring Israel’s war against Gaza to an end. The administration is also trying to uphold a shaky ceasefire that was agreed with Iran to halt the war that began on February 28.
"For three years, we have warned that Sudan was on the brink of catastrophe, and those warnings have gone unanswered," said International Rescue Committee Country Director Richard Data.
Sudan’s recent outbreak of civil war, following years of coups and credible accusations of ethnic cleansing and genocide, persists under the radar.
TRUMP ADMINISTRATION TOUTS MORE THAN $1B IN UN BUDGET CUTS AS REFORM PUSH GAINS MOMENTUM
Members of Sudanese Armed Popular Resistance Force take part in a military parade for fresh graduates, in Al-Qadarif state, in eastern Sudan on May 20, 2026.  (AFP via Getty Images)

The civil war broke out in April 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces led by Gen. Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and Gen. Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, widely known as "Hemedti," leader of the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF).

The two had been in an uneasy alliance ruling the country following the 2019 overthrow of Sudan’s longtime dictator, Omar al-Bashir, who had been in power since 1989. Together, the generals staged another coup in 2021, toppling the interim civilian government that had been in power after the fall of Bashir.
While both the Sudanese Armed Forces and RSF are accused of committing atrocities, recent reports have highlighted the brutality of the RSF.
A major focus of the deteriorating conditions has been in El-Obeid in North Kordofan state, where an escalating hunger crisis is plaguing over 100,000 displaced people in camps throughout the city.
"What we need to do is really now to plan for the scale-up beyond the 100,000 people that we have been supporting," said World Food Programme Sudan Country Director, Abdallah Alwardat.

Members of the Sudanese army's Special Mission Forces batallion in the Northern State hold a parade in Karima city on May 19, 2024. Sudan has been in the throes of conflict for over a year between the regular army led by de facto ruler Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and the RSF led by his former deputy Mohamed Hamdan Daglo.  (AFP via Getty Images)
El Fasher in the Darfur region is another major flashpoint, where the RSF took control in October 2025 and killed more than 6,000 people in the initial siege of the city.

A recent July report from the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights revealed widespread acts of sexual violence against women and girls, some as young as 12, including reports of mass and gang rapes committed by the RSF.
The RSF is also accused of abduction, with survivors describing incidents of girls and women being beaten, having their hands tied behind their backs, and being driven away in a Land cruiser.

Sudanese displaced people gather at the Zam Zam refugee camp outside the town of El-Fashir in the Darfour region of Sudan, during a visit by U.N. officials, on July 1, 2004. The U.N. humanitarian aid and refugee agencies appealed Wednesday, Feb. 7, 2024, for $4.1 billion in international support for embattled civilians in Sudan amid signs that some may be dying of starvation after nearly a year of war there between the forces of rival generals. (AP Photo/Karel Prinsloo, File)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The United Nations and other human rights groups have accused the RSF of perpetrating ethnically targeted attacks and concluded that at least three components of genocide have been overwhelmingly met, including deliberately inflicting conditions of life intended to destroy a group in whole or in part.

A U.N. report from September 2025 found that the Sudanese Armed Forces have also committed war crimes and attacked civilian populations and infrastructure. Both the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces targeted civilians with perceived affiliations to the enemy, executing, torturing and raping victims.

title: Antisemitic violence reaches deadliest level since 1994, new global report finds
summary: The J7 report reveals 20 people were killed in antisemitic attacks in 2025, marking the deadliest year since 1994 with a 97% rise in violence.
story: Cornell Law professor William Jacobson discusses a report finding that rising antisemitism is forcing many Jewish Americans to hide their identity on ‘America Reports.’
A shocking new report says 2025 was the deadliest year for antisemitic attacks worldwide since 1994.

The J7 Large Communities’ Task Force Against Antisemitism released its second annual report, which tracks antisemitic hatred in the seven countries outside of Israel where over 90% of Jews live. According to the report, 20 people were killed in antisemitic attacks in 2025. All of the deadly attacks took place in J7 countries.

The Anti-Defamation League (ADL) is one of two organizations representing the Jewish diaspora in the U.S. in the J7, which includes similar organizations from Australia, Canada, Argentina, the U.S., the U.K., Germany and France.
CHRISTIAN LEADERS HOLD EMERGENCY SUMMIT IN JERUSALEM TO CONFRONT GLOBAL RISE IN ANTISEMITISM
Police cordon off an area at Bondi Beach after a terrorist attack at a Hanukkah celebration in Sydney, Australia, on Dec. 14, 2025. (Mark Baker/AP Photo)
ADL Senior Director of Global Research and Diplomatic Affairs Aykan Erdemir told Fox News Digital that the report’s findings show "there’s no time to waste" in combating hate.

"This isn't a warning sign anymore, it's already happening," Erdemir said. "If governments let antisemitism take root and perpetrators walk free, the violence won't stop with Jewish communities. History shows Jews are the canary in the coal mine: when hatred against Jews rises unchecked, it's an early warning that everyone's safety and rights are at risk."

The J7 report finds that there were over 23,000 antisemitic incidents in J7 countries throughout 2025 – this represented a 97% increase in violent incidents and a 136% increase in total antisemitic incidents since 2022.
The Hamas terror attacks of Oct. 7, 2023, sent antisemitic hate skyrocketing worldwide.
GERMAN OFFICIALS WARN ISLAMIST, FAR-LEFT RHETORIC DRIVING SPIKE IN ANTISEMITIC ATTACKS

Firefighters are seen tackling a blaze at Highfield Road in the Golders Green neighborhood of London, following an arson attack on four charity ambulances belonging to the Jewish Community volunteer Ambulance Service. (PA/PA Images via Getty Images)

According to the report, each of the countries face an environment where antisemitism is "no longer confined to the fringes." Countries are witnessing anti-Zionism associated with the conflict in Gaza becoming "a vehicle for antisemitic expression" and educational institutions becoming an "acute flashpoint" for hatred. Combined with growing online extremism, Jewish people "across the globe report hiding their Jewish identity in public" and questioning "whether they have a future in their home countries."
Individually, the report shows how countries face their own unique challenges in quashing hatred.

A member of the public leaves the scene with her child, who is covered in an emergency blanket, after a terrorist attack at a Hanukkah celebration at Bondi Beach on December 14, 2025, in Sydney, Australia. Australia, which has seen a 270% increase in antisemitic incidents since 2021, was home to the Bondi Beach terror attack in December 2025, during which 15 people were killed. The report says that both Islamist and left-wing extremist threats in the country "need to be prioritized, and dealt with effectively."

In Germany, a 215% increase in antisemitic incidents has been coupled with the highest per capita rate of incidents, with 69.8 incidents per 1,000 Jewish residents in 2025 for a total of 8,725 incidents.
Antisemitic hate on display at an anti-Israel protest in London. Antisemitism in the U.K. is hitting record levels since the Hamas terror attacks on Oct. 7. (Campaign Against Antisemitism on X)

The report said that normalization of hate "remains the most pressing challenge" in Germany, with the rise in incidents attributed to the "confluence of far-right ethno-nationalism, left-wing anti-Zionism, and Islamist extremism simultaneously."

In Canada, which has experienced a 60% rise in antisemitic incidents since 2021, there is a concern that "foreign state interference" is at play, in addition to "the exploitation of domestic institutions by extremist networks."

The U.S. has had a 131% increase in antisemitic incidents since 2021. Though antisemitic incidents declined significantly from 2024, the 6,274 antisemitic incidents tracked in 2025 included 300 reports of physical assault.

France has witnessed a rise in antisemitic incidents of 124% since 2021. The report notes that there is "a growing climate of discrimination" where Jews in France report being refused service, denied contracts and excluded from events.

In the U.K., which has experienced a 64% increase in antisemitic incidents since 2021, 48% of 3,700 antisemitic incidents were motivated by anti-Zionism, and 53% included references to the conflict involving Gaza.
London, UK, Dec 9 2023, anti-Israel protesters hold a banner saying "From the river to the sea." (Andy Soloman/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)

Though the government in Argentina is pro-Israel, the country "has generated conspiratorial antisemitic backlash from the left and from fringe nationalist movements," the report said. Since 2021, Argentina has seen a 46% increase in antisemitic incidents.

The J7 report also added a special chapter on antisemitism in Ireland, which is not a J7 country. While Ireland has only a 2,200-person Jewish community, it has reported 143 incidents of antisemitism. Despite antisemitism in Ireland taking hold "primarily in everyday settings," unlike J7 countries, Ireland has no national plan for combating antisemitism and no security funding for the Jewish population.

He called on law enforcement to "hold perpetrators fully accountable," but said that "the real goal has to be stopping attacks before they happen and preventing Jews from being driven out of public spaces, not just responding once the damage is done."

title: China, Russia, Iran and North Korea form 'axis of aggressors' that could overwhelm US, book warns
summary: A new report documents 616 instances of security cooperation among China, Russia, Iran and North Korea, warning of a dangerous simultaneity problem.
story: FDD report warns America’s adversaries are combining military support, sanctioned energy trade and technology transfers to stretch U.S. defenses.

China, Russia, Iran and North Korea are acting as a strategically aligned bloc even without a formal mutual-defense treaty, according to a new Foundation for Defense of Democracies book warning that their cooperation could leave the United States confronting multiple crises simultaneously.

The book, "Axis of Aggressors: Countering the Cooperation of China, Russia, Iran and North Korea," examines how the four authoritarian governments support one another across military, economic, cyber and technology domains.

Its authors acknowledge that the grouping is not a NATO-style alliance. It has no unified command, comprehensive defense commitment or complete trust among its members. But they argue that its practical effects are already visible in active conflicts.
TRUMP TO CONFRONT XI AT HIGH-STAKES SUMMIT OVER CHINA BACKING FOR IRAN, RUSSIA

In this pool photograph distributed by the Russian state agency Sputnik, Russiain President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un walk before a military parade marking the 80th anniversary of victory over Japan and the end of World War II in Beijing’s Tiananmen Square on Sept. 3, 2025. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian is seen at left in the background. (Sergey Bobylev / POOL / AFP via Getty Images)

"I just got back from a couple of weeks in Ukraine, and when I’m sitting in Ukraine, it’s really obvious to me that Ukraine is fighting Russia, North Korea, Iran and China," retired Rear Adm. Mark Montgomery, one of the book’s three authors, told Fox News Digital.
Montgomery pointed to North Korean ammunition and troops, Iranian drones and production expertise, and Chinese economic and technological support for Moscow.

"China is backstopping the whole thing, providing the economic backstop to Russia’s economy so they can survive this four-year catastrophic event for Russia," Montgomery said. "They’re providing microelectronics that we see in ballistic, cruise and hypersonic missiles."

The book’s researchers documented 616 instances of security cooperation among the four governments from Jan. 1, 2019, through Dec. 31, 2025, including arms transfers, weapons development, military exercises, intelligence sharing and military exchanges.
The central danger, Montgomery said, is what the book calls the "simultaneity problem."
"We don’t get to handle these with a singularity anymore. We have to handle this with a simultaneity," he said. "And I don’t think we can handle two problems at once, much less three or four."

During a potential confrontation between China and Taiwan, Montgomery said, North Korea could threaten South Korea or conduct limited attacks intended to pin down U.S. forces. A conflict involving Russia and NATO’s Baltic members could be accompanied by Iranian terrorism or other hostile activity.
THREE KEY REASONS WHY AMERICA CANNOT AFFORD TO LOSE TAIWAN TO COMMUNIST CHINA

Russian President Vladimir Putin, left, greets Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi prior to their talks at the Kremlin in Moscow, Russia, Monday, June 23, 2025. (Alexander Kazakov, Sputnik, Kremlin Pool Photo via AP)

The book identifies China-Russia military cooperation as the axis’s most consequential bilateral relationship. Chinese dual-use products have helped sustain Russia’s defense industrial base, while Moscow is transferring technology and battlefield lessons that could assist China in a Pacific conflict.

North Korea has supplied Russia with millions of artillery rounds, ballistic missiles and troops, while Moscow has assisted Pyongyang’s missile, space, drone and nuclear programs, according to the book.

Iran has provided Russia with drones and production knowledge. The book warns that Russian and Chinese assistance could also help Tehran rebuild military capabilities damaged during its conflicts with Israel and the United States.
"The longer they can entangle the United States, whether it was in Ukraine or in Iran, China and Russia are the primary beneficiaries," Montgomery said.

Officers and soldiers aboard the Chinese People's Liberation Army PLA Navy's guided-missile destroyer Nanning wave as the ship enters the waters of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region in south China, July 2, 2026. (Ji Peng/Xinhua via Getty Images)
Economic ties underpin the military cooperation, according to co-author Elaine Dezenski, who described the four-country economy as a "fractured alignment."

"These four players are bound together more by necessity than they are by a specific trust or shared strategy among them," Dezenski told Fox News Digital. "China needs energy. Russia and Iran need buyers for their oil and gas. And North Korea needs any lifeline that it can get."
China purchases discounted Russian and Iranian energy while providing goods, technology and access to its domestic market.

The relationships remain unequal. Russia and Iran compete to sell similar products, while China can seek other suppliers. But Dezenski said those divisions should not obscure the benefits the cooperation provides.
"The economics of this very much underpin the foundations for the military engagement that we see," she said.
The book says China purchases as much as 95% of Iran’s oil exports. Some sanctioned oil is routed through third countries, relabeled or processed by independent Chinese refineries known as "teapots."
"The export juggernaut that is China today is fueled by sanctioned oil and gas," Dezenski said.
TRUMP MAY CLAIM HE WON THE FIGHT WITH IRAN, BUT THERE’S A BIGGER WAR ALREADY UNDERWAY

In this Aug. 13, 2007, file photo, a convoy of Chinese APCs rolls by during a rehearsal for a massive joint military exercise by the two former Cold War rivals, the first on Russia's territory in the Chelyabinsk region in Russia's Ural Mountains. Chinese and Russian military forces are engaged in joint exercises through Friday, Aug. 13, 2021, in northwestern China as ties grow between the two autocratic states amid uncertainty over instability in Afghanistan. (AP Photo, File)

Dezenski also warned that China, Russia and Iran are developing payment systems outside traditional Western banking infrastructure. More trade is being settled in yuan through China’s Cross-Border Interbank Payment System, or CIPS, potentially reducing Washington’s ability to enforce sanctions through the dollar system.
"We need to really think about that sooner rather than later, before this alternative payment system becomes too big to tackle," Dezenski said.
Montgomery said the line between criminal hackers and government operatives is often deliberately blurred in all four countries.
"These regimes routinely outsource work to criminal groups to keep their own hands clean, and those groups are increasingly networking with each other," he said.

The book cites ties involving Iranian cybercriminals and Russian ransomware groups, Chinese actors on Russian dark-web forums, and Russian and North Korean state-backed hackers using shared operational infrastructure.

Russian President Vladimir Putin, left, and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, right, examine a launch pad of Soyuz rockets during their meeting at the Vostochny cosmodrome outside the city of Tsiolkovsky, about 125 miles from the city of Blagoveshchensk in the far eastern Amur region of Russia, on Sept. 13, 2023. North Korean leader Kim hailed the country's relationship with Russia on June 12, 2024, as reports suggest that Russian President Putin will soon visit the isolated country for his third meeting with Kim. (Mikhail Metzel, Sputnik, Kremlin Pool Photo via AP, File)

Carrie Filipetti, executive director of the Vandenberg Coalition and a former State Department official during the first Trump administration, said drone warfare demonstrates how assistance moves among the countries.
"Chinese components are used to create Iranian drones, which are then deployed by the Russians against Ukrainian civilians," Filipetti told Fox News Digital.

She said the relationship has also endangered American troops, pointing to the January 2024 Tower 22 attack in Jordan, which killed three U.S. Army Reserve soldiers and wounded more than 40 service members.

"The military and ideological relationship between Russia and Iran is not just a theoretical threat to the United States — American service members have been killed as a result of it," Filipetti said.

Filipetti said the attack used an Iranian drone and Russian tactics developed during the war in Ukraine. "These adversaries don’t agree on everything, but they do on one thing: to reorient the world away from America and the West," she said. "Our service members and citizens will continue to suffer until we treat the threat as the united threat it is."
Retired Air Force Lt. Gen. Richard Newton said the danger stems not only from military modernization in each country, but from the degree to which the four governments are increasingly coordinating.

"I couldn’t agree more with the underlying findings the authors present regarding the rapid military modernization unfolding across multiple domains — air, sea, land, space and cyber — emanating from China, Russia, Iran and North Korea," Newton told Fox News Digital.

A billboard depicting Iran's supreme leaders since 1979: (L to R) Ayatollahs Ruhollah Khomeini (until 1989), Ali Khamenei (until 2026), and Mojtaba Khamenei (incumbent) is displayed above a highway in Tehran on March 10, 2026. Iran marked the appointment of Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei to replace his father as its supreme leader on March 9, 2026. (AFP/Via Getty Images)

"These nation-states represent extraordinary adversarial challenges for the United States. That’s concerning enough," he said. "But a major challenge President Trump is facing in his second administration is the level and degree of integration, synchronization and coordination among these four adversaries, who are more unified today than ever in their collective pursuits to threaten U.S. national security interests."
Newton said the changing character of warfare, demonstrated by more than four years of fighting between Russia and Ukraine and the current U.S.-Iran conflict, has compounded the threat.
"Couple that with the changing nature of warfare we’ve been witnessing," he said, "and the task to defend our nation is now much more complex and daunting."

Retired Air Force Gen. Philip Breedlove, who served as NATO supreme allied commander and commander of U.S. European Command from 2013 to 2016, argued that Washington’s language understates the severity of the confrontation.
"We often say that we are in ‘strategic competition’ with China and Russia. They are at war with us," Breedlove told Fox News Digital.
Breedlove said China, Russia, Iran and North Korea "are not partners looking for cooperation with the U.S.," but governments seeking to "diminish and defeat" American power.
"The enemy gets a vote," Breedlove said. "Our enemies are voting by their support to Russia and Iran."
He added that assistance from the other countries has become increasingly important to Moscow as it struggles to sustain its war.
"Aid is critical to Russia," Breedlove said. "Russia is failing and becoming ever more dependent on its allies."
The authors recommend stronger coordination with allies, expanded defense production, greater protection of U.S. critical infrastructure and more aggressive sanctions enforcement.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The war in Iran has pushed China and Russia closer together. (Sergei Guneev/Reuters)

Dezenski called for targeting the full network supporting sanctioned Russian and Iranian oil, including refineries, ports, insurers and financiers, rather than focusing primarily on individual vessels.
"We need to treat this axis as a threat, as a combined threat," Montgomery said, "that will confront us in every one of our crisis areas."

Efrat (Effie) Lachter is a reporter for Fox News Digital with more than 15 years of experience covering conflict, global affairs, human rights and political accountability. She has directed and produced more than 200 documentary segments across more than 40 countries, documenting conflicts, humanitarian crises, corruption, human trafficking, gender-based violence and the human stories behind major world events.

Lachter’s reporting has taken her into conflict zones and crisis areas across the Middle East, Europe, Asia and Africa. Her work has included uncovering human trafficking networks, revealing an ISIS underground torture prison in Syria, documenting the war in Ukraine and interviewing senior political figures and world leaders. She was also among the Western journalists who entered Russia after the war began to bring testimonies from Putin’s opposition. Lachter is the recipient of the 2022 Peres Center for Peace Award and was a 2023–2024 Knight-Wallace Journalism Fellow at the University of Michigan. She also won two Rockower Awards for Excellence in Reporting. She holds a bachelor's degree in communication and a master's degree in political science.

title: Senate leaders reach a deal to avert a shutdown before the 2026 elections
summary: Senate leaders have struck a bipartisan agreement to keep the government funded past the 2026 midterm elections and avoid a shutdown in October.
story: WASHINGTON — Senate leaders have struck a bipartisan agreement to keep the government funded past the 2026 midterm elections and avoid a politically tricky shutdown in October.
Funding currently expires at the end of Sept. 30, triggering a full government shutdown on Oct. 1 if Congress fails to act.

The continuing resolution, or “CR,” was announced Sunday by Senate Appropriations Committee Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, and Vice Chair Patty Murray, D-Wash. It would keep funds flowing at existing levels until Dec. 11.
The Senate is slated to hold a procedural vote to advance the legislation on Monday, with the goal of passing it this week before the chamber leaves for its August recess.
It would give time for congressional leaders to pursue a longer-term solution after the midterm elections, when the results will likely shape the direction of the next full-year funding package.

But first, it will need to pass the House, which has already left Washington for the August recess and returns in early September. House Republicans passed their own funding bill through Dec. 4, and the two chambers will need to work out their differences.

Collins said the Senate stopgap bill is “straightforward” and avoids “poison pills” while attaching “necessary adjustments” for the SNAP and WIC food programs, as well as disaster relief and national security programs.

“This measure gives Congress the time we need to continue our work on bipartisan appropriations bills, which are always my strong preference for handling annual government funding,” said Collins, who faces a competitive re-election bid in Maine this fall and has touted her ability to reach bipartisan deals on government funding in making her case to voters.

Murray said the bill fixes issues Democrats had with the House-passed version and “rejects Trump’s frivolous war spending wish list.” She said it closes “loopholes” for the administration to transfer funds from existing programs to Border Patrol, which she said “desperately needs reform, not more money.” And she said it blocks implementation of a proposal by the White House budget office that would “allow Trump officials to cancel grants at any time for any reason.”
“It’s good that we were able to produce a much-improved CR to keep the government funded and avert a shutdown that no one wants,” Murray said in a statement.
The legislation was negotiated with input from top party leaders in the Senate. Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., called it “a responsible path forward.”

“I thank Senator Murray for her tireless work on this deal and her success blocking Trump’s disgraceful efforts to further politicize all federal grants,” Schumer said in a statement. “Democrats remain committed to funding negotiations that help hardworking Americans get ahead and stymie Trump’s wasteful, corrupt agenda that has failed families.”
Rep. Rosa DeLauro, the top Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee, also praised the Senate bill as “a clear improvement over the House Republican continuing resolution.”

title: ‘Spider-Man’ scores biggest opening weekend in box office history, overtaking ‘Avengers: Endgame’
summary: The two blockbusters together pulled in more than $400 million at the domestic box office this weekend.
story: “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” swung to the top of the box office charts with a whopping $360 million debut — the biggest opening weekend in domestic box office history.

Combined with the ongoing draw of Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey,” which pulled in another $51 million this weekend, the two blockbusters delivered a one-two punch that made this the biggest box office weekend ever.

“It reminds me a bit of the Barbenheimer phenomenon, where you had two movies creating this fervor around moviegoing, and that plays very well,” said Paul Dergarabedian, head of marketplace trends at box office analytics company Rentrak.
Together, the two films’ weekend outpaced the box office record set by “Avengers: Endgame,” which opened to $357 million in 2019.
The hype for Sony and Marvel’s “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” is a worldwide phenomenon: The film amassed $932 million globally in its opening weekend alone.

It’s the fourth installment in the Tom Holland-led iteration of the franchise within the Marvel Cinematic Universe. The star-studded movie racked up a 90% critic approval score and a 98% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes.

Anticipation for Nolan’s “The Odyssey,” meanwhile, ran so high that many fans ordered their tickets more than a year in advance, while others scrambled for resold tickets or settled for 2 a.m. showings just to get in.

Dergarabedian said the numbers signal that the tides have once again turned for movie theaters, which in recent years struggled to bounce back from lower post-pandemic attendance, Hollywood labor strikes and the increasing dominance of streaming.
But in recent years, theaters have begun to make a comeback by turning new releases into social events with themed merchandise and opportunities to dress up.

“It’s unbelievable, when you think about it, that we could even get to a number like this,” Dergarabedian said. “I never thought we’d see another $400 million weekend overall, and I never thought we’d see another $300 million opener domestically. It seemed like an insurmountable mountain to climb.”

He said the success of these two films caps an “incredible” year for movie theaters overall: “The Super Mario Galaxy Movie,” “Michael” and “Toy Story 5” have each grossed more than $1 billion, while smaller films like “Obsession” and “Backrooms” have also fueled interest in moviegoing — particularly among young people.
All of this sets up a likely $4 billion summer and $10 billion year, Dergarabedian said, which could make 2026 the highest-grossing summer and the highest-grossing year since 2019.

“The movie theater has become like the go-to outside-the-home place for entertainment, and there’s no denying it,” he said. “So many people have counted out the movie theater for so long. I think this puts to rest any notion that people don’t want to go to the movie theater. They absolutely do.”

title: Ariana Grande to step back from public life following ‘scrutiny’
summary: The singer and actor, who is on tour, will no longer star in the London revival of “Sunday in the Park With George,” which is set to open in summer 2027.
story: Ariana Grande plans to step away from the public eye following scrutiny, the singer’s representative said, as discussion swirls around her health.

The representative confirmed to NBC News that Grande will take “a step back from visibility after she completes the Eternal Sunshine Tour,” which will wrap next month. The statement was first reported by People.

Following the announcement, Empire Street Productions confirmed that Grande has “decided to step back” from the revival of Stephen Sondheim’s “Sunday in the Park With George,” which will open at the Barbican Center in London next summer.

Grande was set to star as both Dot and Marie in the musical, opposite her “Wicked” co-star Jonathan Bailey.
“We know this cannot have been an easy decision, and she makes it with our complete understanding and support,” the production company said. “We wish her nothing but the best.”
The company said that the production will continue as planned and that new casting will be announced “in due course.”
Grande’s Eternal Sunshine Tour, promoting the 2024 album of the same name, will conclude in London on Sept. 1.

“She looks forward to finishing the tour and ending it on a high note, both healthily and happily, and then taking a much-deserved break from public-facing work and appearances, which has led to endless, ongoing public scrutiny,” the representative said in the statement. “This tour has been a beautiful experience for her. She loves her fans and has loved every minute of this tour so much.”

A source close to Grande told NBC News that she “performs a very physical show and there is a lot of athleticism involved. She performs healthily and successfully at a very high level night after night.”

Grande’s health has been a topic of public discussion for several years. Last year, she addressed criticism of her appearance that amassed around the release of “Wicked: For Good.” At the time, she shared a 2024 interview in which she said that in society, “there’s a comfortability that we shouldn’t have, at all,” including commenting on how other people look, calling it “dangerous for all parties involved.”

Grande released her eighth album, “Petal,” on Friday. In an interview with Apple Music, she said it feels “very experimental and different,” adding that she tapped into the “unfiltered rage that I think we all feel sometimes.”

Public discourse around Grande’s body increased after the release of the music video for the title track. Grande portrays an actor named Pepper, who is repeatedly declared “not good enough” by casting executives in auditions before she kills them with a chain saw. As the video ends, a director yells “cut,” and Grande walks off the set, where she is praised for her talent.

Grande is next scheduled to appear in the film “Focker-in-Law” alongside Ben Stiller and Robert De Niro. The “Meet the Parents” franchise movie has a Nov. 25 release date and will be distributed by Universal Pictures — which shares Comcast as a parent company with NBC News.
CORRECTION (Aug. 3, 2026, 12:53 a.m. ET): A previous version of this article misstated the name of Ariana Grande’s new album. It is “Petal,” not “Petals.”

title: Michigan’s primary reflects a Democratic base transforming in Trump 2.0: From the Politics Desk
summary: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.
story: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.

In today’s edition, Sahil Kapur digs into the broader stakes of tomorrow’s Michigan Democratic Senate primary. Plus, we have the latest on Todd Blanche’s attorney general nomination ahead of a key committee vote.
Sign up to receive this newsletter in your inbox every weekday here.
— Adam Wollner
Michigan’s primary reflects a Democratic base transforming in Trump 2.0
Eight years ago, Democrats Haley Stevens and Abdul El-Sayed both ran for office in Michigan.

Stevens won her 2018 House race, while El-Sayed lost his primary for governor. Stevens’ brand of politics was ascendant: a middle-of-the-road Democrat preaching experience, moderation and results. El-Sayed’s pitch for transformative change and universal healthcare fell short in the purple state.

Tomorrow, the two will square off in a hotly contested Senate primary with huge national implications for the rest of Donald Trump’s presidency — and beyond. Both have stayed true to their 2018 brands. And now, El-Sayed has led Stevens by double digits in several recent polls. Such a result would highlight how much the political landscape has transformed since the last midterm in which Trump was in office.
When asked what changed between 2018 and 2026, El-Sayed strategist Rebecca Katz told NBC News, “Trump won again.”

In 2018, Democrats largely saw Trump as an anomaly and trusted the party establishment to deal with him. They successfully recruited a series of center-left candidates across the country, Stevens included, to capture Republican-held seats in competitive areas. Two years later, Joe Biden won the presidency after promising Democrats that if he won, the GOP would have an “epiphany” and relegate Trump to the dustbin of history.

Trump’s decisive victory in 2024 shattered that illusion. The Democratic base is now less trusting of its leaders, and more interested in elevating combative outsiders running on upending the system rather than working within its confines. Add to it the growing economic pain of inflation and what liberals perceive as rising authoritarianism in the GOP, and there is an agitation for a new kind of politics.
Enter El-Sayed.

The Democratic establishment is fighting back, with Stevens locking in endorsements from Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, outgoing Sen. Gary Peters, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and Rep. James Clyburn, D-S.C. The primary will test their influence.
Meanwhile, El-Sayed has secured support from progressive leaders who share his vision, including Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y.

Even if El-Sayed wins tomorrow’s primary, his fight is only just beginning. His progressive vision has had successes this year in deep-blue areas like New York City and Denver. But can it win a general election in battleground Michigan?

The question carries massive stakes for the future of his movement. If El-Sayed is nominated and loses this fall, the center-left will claim validation. But if El-Sayed wins the seat, it’ll fuel the segment of the party that dares to dream big about sending an unabashed progressive to the White House in 2028.

Acting AG Todd Blanche reaches deal with Senate holdouts

After a weekslong standoff between senators and the Trump administration, acting Attorney General Todd Blanche announced that the parties had reached a deal and that he had issued an order “officially” rescinding a $1.8 billion “anti-weaponization” fund.
Blanche had faced pushback from key GOP Sens. John Cornyn of Texas, and Thom Tillis of North Carolina, who said their support for him hinged on the administration’s rescinding its plans for the fund.

In a joint statement, Tillis and Cornyn said that they are “pleased that the Department of Justice has issued a formal order terminating the anti-weaponization fund” and said they “look forward to voting to advance his nomination out of the Senate Judiciary Committee soon.”
The Senate Judiciary Committee is set to vote on Blanche’s nomination to be attorney general in a permanent capacity tomorrow.
Blanche had testified before Congress that the fund was dead, but President Donald Trump threatened over the weekend to “push hard” to revive it.

title: Ethics panel recommends censure for GOP congressman for ‘inappropriate conduct’
summary: The House Ethics Committee is recommending that Rep. Chuck Edwards, R-N.C., be censured by after finding that he engaged “inappropriate conduct towards two young female staffers.”
story: WASHINGTON — The House Ethics Committee said Monday it is recommending that Rep. Chuck Edwards, R-N.C., be censured by the full House after finding that he “engaged in persistent unprofessional and inappropriate conduct towards two young female staffers.”

“The Committee found that Representative Edwards violated the House Code of Official Conduct by failing to adhere to the spirit of rules prohibiting sexual harassment of and unwanted advances to House staffers,” the Ethics Committee said in its 25-page report following a months-long investigation into allegations against Edwards.

The bipartisan panel, led by Chairman Michael Guest, R-Miss., and the ranking member, Rep. Mark DeSalnier, D-Calif., said Edwards denied that any of his actions were intended to be sexual or romantic in nature. He cooperated with the investigation, according to the report.

And the committee said it found no evidence that the congressman engaged in sexual activity with or propositioned any of his staffers. It also concluded that the allegations against Edwards “do not implicate quid pro quo sexual harassment” or violate “the ‘letter’ of federal sexual harassment law.”

But the panel added that “his pattern of behavior would lead a reasonable observer to interpret it as such, including providing the young women with lavish and recurrent gifts, making comments regarding their appearance and dress, inviting them to intimate dinners and vacations, sending notes regarding his effusive affection, and inviting them to other activities as a way to spend time together.”

The committee added in its report: Edwards “has also refused to acknowledge the reality of the power imbalance between a Member of Congress and young staffers, even as his former staffers have been put through this difficult and emotional process with serious repercussions on their personal and professional lives. This shows a lack of self-awareness and accountability.”

Later in the report, the panel added: The Committee is concerned that the House regrettably lost two staffers because of Representative Edwards’ conduct. In this environment, where Members of Congress hold substantial influence, many individuals are reluctant to report misconduct when balancing the fear of reprisal against the potential for accountability.”

Edwards, 65, has not been in Congress long. A former state lawmaker, he ousted then-Rep. Madison Cawthorn in the GOP primary in 2022 but kept a low profile on Capitol Hill, unlike his predecessor, prior to the Ethics probe.

A censure is a formal disapproval by the House, but it’s a political black eye for a vulnerable member like Edwards. Cook Political Report has rated his race against Democrat Jamie Ager as “Lean Republican,” and Ager has significantly outraised Edwards this cycle.
The House is on its long summer recess, so a censure vote could not happen until September at the earliest.

Edwards’ office referred a request for comment to his campaign, which did not immediately respond. Edwards previously called the allegations “baseless” and said in a statement to NBC News in May that he welcomed an investigation.
His counsel wrote a 15-page rebuttal to the committee’s findings, calling them “unfounded.”

“Representative Edwards emphasizes that he has endeavored to comply with all applicable laws regarding his conduct during his time as a Member of Congress and before. Once more, he states his sincere regret if his conduct caused any staff member discomfort or was unwelcome,” they wrote.

The report detailed countless examples of strange and inappropriate behavior by Edwards. The two young women in the ethics report had worked for Edwards at the statehouse in Raleigh and joined his team in Washington after he was elected to Congress.

It said he lavished the two staffers with gifts, including “jewelry totaling over $1,000, designer purses, guns, shoes, flowers, a laptop and cell phone, KitchenAid mixer, robotic vacuum, vacations, tickets to performances, and one-on-one dinners.”
In one example, Edwards paid for one of the women, identified as “Staffer 2” and her friend to visit New York after the staffer’s breakup and bought them tickets to the musical “Hamilton.”
Staffer 2 also said she felt “obligated to wear” a necklace Edwards bought her. When she stopped wearing it, he commented how “disappointed” he was, she testified to the committee.

In another episode outlined in the report, Edwards brought Staffer 1 to a White House holiday event, hid the details from other staffers, bought her flowers, and texted her he was “so excited about tonight” and wanted the evening to be “perfect.” He then pressured her to continue the evening with him, Staffer 1 testified, something the congressman said he could not recall saying.
The committee said he also talked to Staffer 1 and others about going to strip clubs in Washington, D.C., citing interviews with four staffers.
The committee also said Edwards went to Staffer 2’s home to perform chores like yard work; one time, he went there to help decorate her Christmas tree and skipped House votes to do so.
“Here’s another offer I hope you’ll take me up on, unless you’ve made other arrangements,” Edwards texted her. “What if I skip votes and help you decorate your tree once you get home tomorrow?”

Edwards also wrote poems for Staffer 2, the committee said, including one that he read at her going-away party in his congressional office that was accompanied by a slideshow. He cried, and several staffers testified they felt uncomfortable.
The committee released a 60-page appendix of messages between Edwards and Staffers 1 and 2, as well as some photos of gifts he gave them.

Although Edwards provided the committee with some of the text messages between him and the two staffers, “many relevant messages were omitted and/or seemingly deleted from his phone,” the report said.
“When asked about the missing text messages, he testified that he would delete messages ‘at a whim’” and that he used multiple phones, the committee said.

According to the report, Edwards testified to the committee: “I wrote sexual harassment policy [in the corporate world]. I investigated sexual harassment many, many times. I lived a very cautious life.”

title: 18-year-old educator sets Guinness World Record for youngest male college professor
summary: At 18 years old, Nathan Thomas walked into a lecture hall at Miami Dade College in August 2023, like many others his age.
story: At 18 years old, Nathan Thomas walked into a lecture hall at Miami Dade College in August 2023, like many others his age.
Except that Thomas wasn’t a freshman. He was the professor.
His role at Miami Dade College earned him an even greater title, revealed Monday. According to Guinness World Records, he is the youngest-ever male professor.
In August 2023, Thomas was 18 years and 346 days old. He beat a 306-year-old record, held by 19-year-old Colin Maclaurin.

At the time, he was also just barely (16 days) younger than Alia Sabur, who claimed the title of youngest female professor when she stood in front of a classroom in 2008 at 18 years and 362 days old. According to Guinness, she was a full-time faculty member of the department of advanced technology fusion at Konkuk University in Seoul, South Korea.

Thomas had already earned his bachelor’s and master’s degrees in electrical engineering, both with honors, according to Guinness. He enrolled in Miami Dade College when he was 10 years old, before transferring at 14 to Florida International University, which is where he earned both degrees.
Thomas then took his talents to COP 2270: C for Engineers in 2023, which the record counter described as “complex computing and programming lessons.”
“Once you’re in that setting, everyone’s there for the same reason, which is to learn,” he told Guinness. “Age doesn’t really factor into that.”
“I just focus on trying to do my job well and helping students in whatever way I can. If someone’s willing to put in the effort, that’s really all that matters to me,” he added.
Thomas said he was drawn to STEM partly because both his parents are engineers, and because math always “clicked” for him, he told Guinness.
His mother “had a way of making things feel simple even when they weren’t, and I think some of that stuck with me more than I realized at the time,” he said.
He noted that his favorite thing about teaching is watching students experience the material “click” for them as it did for him.

“It’s a different kind of satisfaction than solving a problem yourself, almost like getting to relive that feeling through someone else,” Thomas continued. “Teaching something forces you to understand it on a whole other level — so I end up learning just as much from it as the students do, if not more.”

He has since enrolled in the University of Miami School of Law to earn his juris doctor degree. According to Guinness, he is still teaching online courses and plans to graduate with his law degree in 2028.

title: Michigan reports first two deaths in the cyclosporiasis outbreak
summary: Two people in Michigan who had contracted cyclosporiasis have died, the state Health and Human Services Department said Monday.
story: Two people in Michigan who had contracted cyclosporiasis have died, the state Health and Human Services Department said Monday.
Both people — whose identities were not provided — had “significant underlying health conditions that may have been impacted by cyclosporiasis and dehydration,” according to a news release.

Cyclospora, the parasite found in human feces that causes cyclosporiasis, can lead to dehydration because of the loss of fluid through severe diarrhea and vomiting, said Dr. William Schaffner, an infectious disease specialist at Vanderbilt University Medical Center.
The illness is often treated with Bactrim, an antibiotic, although many people with healthy immune systems often recover on their own, he said.
State health officials said no additional information will be provided on the two cases.
“Cyclosporiasis is generally not a life-threatening illness. Death resulting from cyclosporiasis is uncommon in the United States,” it said in the release.
A spokesperson for the Food and Drug Administration said the agency is aware of the two deaths.

“Based on information provided to FDA by the state of Michigan, both of these individuals had illness onset dates prior to the date of Taylor Farms de Mexico’s voluntary recall on July 17, 2026,” the spokesperson said via email Monday. Taylor Farms de Mexico is the produce supplier linked to contaminated lettuce at Taco Bell.
The deaths come amid an unusually severe cyclosporiasis season with cases reported in 45 states, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
More than 11,000 cases of the foodborne illness have been confirmed in Michigan and 193 people have been hospitalized since early May, according to the state health department.

The outbreaks in Michigan and nine other states have been linked to lettuce at Taco Bell that was supplied by Taylor Farms and sourced from central Mexico. Last month, Taylor Farms de Mexico issued a voluntary recall of all iceberg lettuce supplied from central Mexico.

title: Senate leaders reach a deal to avert a shutdown before the 2026 elections
summary: Senate leaders have struck a bipartisan agreement to keep the government funded past the 2026 midterm elections and avoid a shutdown in October.
story: WASHINGTON — Senate leaders have struck a bipartisan agreement to keep the government funded past the 2026 midterm elections and avoid a politically tricky shutdown in October.
Funding currently expires at the end of Sept. 30, triggering a full government shutdown on Oct. 1 if Congress fails to act.

The continuing resolution, or “CR,” was announced Sunday by Senate Appropriations Committee Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, and Vice Chair Patty Murray, D-Wash. It would keep funds flowing at existing levels until Dec. 11.
The Senate is slated to hold a procedural vote to advance the legislation on Monday, with the goal of passing it this week before the chamber leaves for its August recess.
It would give time for congressional leaders to pursue a longer-term solution after the midterm elections, when the results will likely shape the direction of the next full-year funding package.

But first, it will need to pass the House, which has already left Washington for the August recess and returns in early September. House Republicans passed their own funding bill through Dec. 4, and the two chambers will need to work out their differences.

Collins said the Senate stopgap bill is “straightforward” and avoids “poison pills” while attaching “necessary adjustments” for the SNAP and WIC food programs, as well as disaster relief and national security programs.

“This measure gives Congress the time we need to continue our work on bipartisan appropriations bills, which are always my strong preference for handling annual government funding,” said Collins, who faces a competitive re-election bid in Maine this fall and has touted her ability to reach bipartisan deals on government funding in making her case to voters.

Murray said the bill fixes issues Democrats had with the House-passed version and “rejects Trump’s frivolous war spending wish list.” She said it closes “loopholes” for the administration to transfer funds from existing programs to Border Patrol, which she said “desperately needs reform, not more money.” And she said it blocks implementation of a proposal by the White House budget office that would “allow Trump officials to cancel grants at any time for any reason.”
“It’s good that we were able to produce a much-improved CR to keep the government funded and avert a shutdown that no one wants,” Murray said in a statement.
The legislation was negotiated with input from top party leaders in the Senate. Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., called it “a responsible path forward.”

“I thank Senator Murray for her tireless work on this deal and her success blocking Trump’s disgraceful efforts to further politicize all federal grants,” Schumer said in a statement. “Democrats remain committed to funding negotiations that help hardworking Americans get ahead and stymie Trump’s wasteful, corrupt agenda that has failed families.”
Rep. Rosa DeLauro, the top Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee, also praised the Senate bill as “a clear improvement over the House Republican continuing resolution.”

title: Naked man who jumped off Brooklyn Bridge and survived is arrested and charged
summary: A 44-year-old man was arrested after climbing to the top of New York City’s historic Brooklyn Bridge on Sunday, displaying flags and eventually plunging into the water, police said.
story: A 44-year-old man was arrested after climbing to the top of New York City’s historic Brooklyn Bridge on Sunday, displaying flags and eventually plunging into the water, police said.

Galymzhan Abaildayev is facing charges of reckless endangerment, graffiti, public lewdness, criminal trespass and disorderly conduct, the New York Police Department said in a statement to NBC News on Monday. It’s unclear whether he has retained an attorney.

Police were called to the Brooklyn Bridge on Sunday afternoon after reports that a man was scaling the 143-year-old bridge with a backpack. Abaildayev allegedly stripped down after reaching the top of the bridge’s north tower.
He then jumped from the top of the bridge’s tower into the East River, where police said he was rescued by the department’s harbor unit. He was then taken to a city hospital in stable condition.

The Brooklyn Bridge has a clearance of 135 feet from the water at its center, according to New York City’s Department of Transportation. The city does not detail the exact height of the towers, but a company that worked on restoration of the bridge noted that the towers are 272-feet tall.
Abaildayev had a backpack and two flags with him, according to police. The police department did not provide additional information as to what was on the flags.

title: ‘Exorcist’ star Linda Blair’s home searched over ‘kennel operation,’ Los Angeles officials say
summary: “The Exorcist” star Linda Blair’s home in Southern California was searched by animal control officials in connection with a “kennel operation,” authorities said.
story: “The Exorcist” star Linda Blair’s home in Southern California was searched by animal control officials in connection with a “kennel operation,” authorities said.

Blair’s home was searched Friday under an inspection warrant by the Los Angeles County Department of Animal Care and Control (DACC) and the Los Angeles County Department of Regional Planning, officials said in a statement.
The 67-year-old actor, who runs a dog adoption charity, has not been accused of committing any crimes.
“The goal is to inspect this property for buildings and structures associated with a kennel operation reported to have more than 100 dogs,” the department said in the statement.
Permits for the facility had expired in 2023 and attempts to contact the owner had gone unanswered, it added.
“The warrant allows us to lawfully access the property and verify compliance with County codes,” the department added.
Blair appeared to confirm the inspection in a video she posted to her Instagram account on Friday.
“I just wanted to check in because today we got a really big surprise visit, and as it turns out, there is nothing but some paperwork and some new diagrams and things,” she said.
Blair, best known for playing Regan MacNeil in the 1973 horror classic “The Exorcist,” won a Golden Globe and was nominated for an Academy Award for best supporting actress.
The actor has long been an animal rights activist. In 2003, she started a nonprofit, the Linda Blair WorldHeart Foundation, that focuses in rehabilitating dogs and facilitate their adoption.

“It’s a big crisis we’re dealing with in California and across the country, so any and all support would mean the world,” she said in her video. “The rest of us are just taking care of our chores every single day, and what commitment we’ve already given to the animals. And I hope everybody will do the same and be supportive. But I want to let you know I’m OK, and so are the animals.”
The DACC declined to say how many animals were found on the property.

“As this is an active and ongoing investigation, DACC is not able to answer specific questions about this case at this time,” the department said. “DACC appreciates the public’s concern and want to assure everyone that the Department is committed to ensuring all kennel operations meet legal requirements and provide humane care.”

At least 128 dogs are listed as available for adoption on the Linda Blair WorldHeart Foundation’s website. It is not clear whether all of the dogs are currently living at the property authorities searched this week.

title: Phil Collins says he nearly died in 2024 after years of alcohol abuse
summary: Years of alcohol abuse brought rock icon Phil Collins to death’s door two years ago, with loved ones rushing to his bedside “to say goodbye,” the legendary singer and drummer said in an interview published over the weekend.
story: Years of alcohol abuse brought rock icon Phil Collins to death’s door two years ago, with loved ones rushing to his bedside “to say goodbye,” the legendary singer and drummer said in an interview published over the weekend.

The Genesis front man had been admitted to a Swiss hospital to treat his alcohol addiction. He was released in late 2023 and then re-admitted months later; he landed in the intensive care unit, where he was unconscious for long stretches of time.
His long-time manager summoned Collins’ family, fearing the rock icon was about to die.

“Because there were some decisions to be made about ‘Do we keep Phil on life support?’ kind of thing,” Collins told The Times of London in an interview Saturday night.

“My kidneys were packing up, my organs were just seizing up. People were coming to say goodbye. But I don’t remember them coming, I didn’t have no idea this was going on. They were all worried that they wouldn’t see me again. It could all have gone so terribly wrong.”
Collins said he’s now on the mend following that seven-month stay in the hospital.
“I was very lucky to have come out of that,” Collins said. “Needless to say, I haven’t had a drink since.”
The Collins family celebrated the end of 2025 by renting out an entire floor of the Mandarin Oriental in the Knightsbridge neighborhood of London, an opportunity to catch up and celebrate.

He vividly recalled how his daughter, “Emily in Paris” star Lily Collins, “was sitting beside me in tears, saying, ‘I never thought I’d get these moments.’ We had an incredible time. I can’t overemphasize how fantastic it was,” he said.
The 75-year-old musician has said he’s also been facing mobility issues lately, making it hard to get back on stage. He’s been frequently seen using crutches in recent public appearances.
“I had five operations on my knee now,” Phil explained on the BBC’s “Eras” podcast in January. “I’ve got a knee that works and I can walk, albeit with assistance (from) crutches.”
The decades he’s spent playing the drums have also taken a significant toll on the eight-time Grammy winner and Rock & Roll Hall of Famer.

“If I can’t do what I did as well as I did it, I’d rather relax and not do anything. If I wake up one day and I can hold a pair of drumsticks, then I will have a crack at it. But I just feel like I’ve used up my air miles,” he said in a 2024 documentary “Phil Collins: Drummer First.”

title: Mauricio Pochettino to return as U.S. Soccer coach for 2030 World Cup
summary: Mauricio Pochettino agreed to remain U.S. Soccer’s men’s national team coach through the 2030 World Cup, insisting there’s “tremendous potential” to bring America to the sport’s upper echelons, officials said Monday.
story: Mauricio Pochettino agreed to remain U.S. Soccer’s men’s national team coach through the 2030 World Cup, insisting there’s “tremendous potential” to bring America to the sport’s upper echelons, officials said Monday.
The new contract to keep Pochettino in red, white and blue came less than a month after the 54-year-old Argentine led the U.S. to the round of 16 in the 2026 World Cup, played on home soil.

“Mauricio and his staff believe in the future of soccer in the United States and our new project allows us to build on progress of the USMNT and the momentum of U.S. Soccer,” U.S. Soccer CEO and Secretary-General JT Batson said in a statement.

“We know we have a lot of work to do to achieve our clear ambitions, including competing to win Men’s World Cups and having soccer become the most played sport in every community,” the statement said. “I couldn’t be more excited that Mauricio and team are committed to partnering with all of us to do the hard work to bring those ambitions to life.”
While the Americans failed to make it to the quarterfinals, Pochettino insisted his team’s World Cup run “only strengthened our belief in what is possible here.”

“Working together with U.S. Soccer over the past two years, it has become clear to us that there is tremendous potential to make the Men’s National Team program even stronger,” Pochettino said in a statement released by U.S. Soccer.

The statement added: “The passion we experienced from the fans throughout the World Cup only strengthened our belief in what is possible here. We are excited by the opportunity to bring all our experience and knowledge to even more areas of U.S. Soccer while helping strengthen the pathways for players, coaches and teams across the Federation. We want to try to have a lasting impact on the sport in the country that has welcomed us so warmly and for that impact to extend beyond results on the field.”
From Chelsea to Paris Saint-Germain, Pochettino coached several of the world’s highest-profile clubs but had never led a national team before taking over the U.S. men’s program in 2024.
Early U.S. men’s national team results for the former Tottenham boss were mixed, with a 15-10-1 record entering the World Cup as he tested multiple lineup combinations.

His attacking style quickly earned praise once the tournament opened, as the U.S. won its group and scored a team record for goals. The U.S. beat Bosnia-Herzegovina in the knockout round of 32 before exiting in the round of 16 to Belgium in a deflating 4-1 defeat.

After that loss, Pochettino expressed gratitude for the working relationship he had built with the leadership of U.S. Soccer, which had offered a contract extension to the coach before the tournament.

Though he declared himself an Argentine first and foremost, Pochettino didn’t shy away from ingratiating himself with U.S. fans by singing the team’s chosen song of the tournament, John Denver’s “Take Me Home, Country Roads,” on the pitch after matches.

The new deal allows the U.S. to retain a highly regarded coach in hopes that the team can continue the improvement Pochettino said he had seen take place over the previous year. Pochettino said last month that the U.S. had been a “mess” after the 2025 Gold Cup.
“I am so proud because in one year … this team show that we can play football, we can play soccer, we can compete,” Pochettino said July 5. “We need to keep improving.”

Terms of Pochettino’s deal were not disclosed, but his initial deal was reportedly worth around $6 million annually in base salary, which was already the largest deal earned by any coach in U.S. soccer history.
To afford it, and lure Pochettino away from club jobs in 2024, U.S. Soccer rounded up private investors such as Ken Griffin to help pay.
The 2030 World Cup will be co-hosted by defending champion Spain, Portugal and Morocco with some early matches in Uruguay, Pochettino’s native Argentina and Paraguay.

title: Ethics panel recommends censure for GOP congressman for ‘inappropriate conduct’
summary: The House Ethics Committee is recommending that Rep. Chuck Edwards, R-N.C., be censured by after finding that he engaged “inappropriate conduct towards two young female staffers.”
story: WASHINGTON — The House Ethics Committee said Monday it is recommending that Rep. Chuck Edwards, R-N.C., be censured by the full House after finding that he “engaged in persistent unprofessional and inappropriate conduct towards two young female staffers.”

“The Committee found that Representative Edwards violated the House Code of Official Conduct by failing to adhere to the spirit of rules prohibiting sexual harassment of and unwanted advances to House staffers,” the Ethics Committee said in its 25-page report following a months-long investigation into allegations against Edwards.

The bipartisan panel, led by Chairman Michael Guest, R-Miss., and the ranking member, Rep. Mark DeSalnier, D-Calif., said Edwards denied that any of his actions were intended to be sexual or romantic in nature. He cooperated with the investigation, according to the report.

And the committee said it found no evidence that the congressman engaged in sexual activity with or propositioned any of his staffers. It also concluded that the allegations against Edwards “do not implicate quid pro quo sexual harassment” or violate “the ‘letter’ of federal sexual harassment law.”

But the panel added that “his pattern of behavior would lead a reasonable observer to interpret it as such, including providing the young women with lavish and recurrent gifts, making comments regarding their appearance and dress, inviting them to intimate dinners and vacations, sending notes regarding his effusive affection, and inviting them to other activities as a way to spend time together.”

The committee added in its report: Edwards “has also refused to acknowledge the reality of the power imbalance between a Member of Congress and young staffers, even as his former staffers have been put through this difficult and emotional process with serious repercussions on their personal and professional lives. This shows a lack of self-awareness and accountability.”

Later in the report, the panel added: The Committee is concerned that the House regrettably lost two staffers because of Representative Edwards’ conduct. In this environment, where Members of Congress hold substantial influence, many individuals are reluctant to report misconduct when balancing the fear of reprisal against the potential for accountability.”

Edwards, 65, has not been in Congress long. A former state lawmaker, he ousted then-Rep. Madison Cawthorn in the GOP primary in 2022 but kept a low profile on Capitol Hill, unlike his predecessor, prior to the Ethics probe.

A censure is a formal disapproval by the House, but it’s a political black eye for a vulnerable member like Edwards. Cook Political Report has rated his race against Democrat Jamie Ager as “Lean Republican,” and Ager has significantly outraised Edwards this cycle.
The House is on its long summer recess, so a censure vote could not happen until September at the earliest.

Edwards’ office referred a request for comment to his campaign, which did not immediately respond. Edwards previously called the allegations “baseless” and said in a statement to NBC News in May that he welcomed an investigation.
His counsel wrote a 15-page rebuttal to the committee’s findings, calling them “unfounded.”

“Representative Edwards emphasizes that he has endeavored to comply with all applicable laws regarding his conduct during his time as a Member of Congress and before. Once more, he states his sincere regret if his conduct caused any staff member discomfort or was unwelcome,” they wrote.

The report detailed countless examples of strange and inappropriate behavior by Edwards. The two young women in the ethics report had worked for Edwards at the statehouse in Raleigh and joined his team in Washington after he was elected to Congress.

It said he lavished the two staffers with gifts, including “jewelry totaling over $1,000, designer purses, guns, shoes, flowers, a laptop and cell phone, KitchenAid mixer, robotic vacuum, vacations, tickets to performances, and one-on-one dinners.”
In one example, Edwards paid for one of the women, identified as “Staffer 2” and her friend to visit New York after the staffer’s breakup and bought them tickets to the musical “Hamilton.”
Staffer 2 also said she felt “obligated to wear” a necklace Edwards bought her. When she stopped wearing it, he commented how “disappointed” he was, she testified to the committee.

In another episode outlined in the report, Edwards brought Staffer 1 to a White House holiday event, hid the details from other staffers, bought her flowers, and texted her he was “so excited about tonight” and wanted the evening to be “perfect.” He then pressured her to continue the evening with him, Staffer 1 testified, something the congressman said he could not recall saying.
The committee said he also talked to Staffer 1 and others about going to strip clubs in Washington, D.C., citing interviews with four staffers.
The committee also said Edwards went to Staffer 2’s home to perform chores like yard work; one time, he went there to help decorate her Christmas tree and skipped House votes to do so.
“Here’s another offer I hope you’ll take me up on, unless you’ve made other arrangements,” Edwards texted her. “What if I skip votes and help you decorate your tree once you get home tomorrow?”

Edwards also wrote poems for Staffer 2, the committee said, including one that he read at her going-away party in his congressional office that was accompanied by a slideshow. He cried, and several staffers testified they felt uncomfortable.
The committee released a 60-page appendix of messages between Edwards and Staffers 1 and 2, as well as some photos of gifts he gave them.

Although Edwards provided the committee with some of the text messages between him and the two staffers, “many relevant messages were omitted and/or seemingly deleted from his phone,” the report said.
“When asked about the missing text messages, he testified that he would delete messages ‘at a whim’” and that he used multiple phones, the committee said.

According to the report, Edwards testified to the committee: “I wrote sexual harassment policy [in the corporate world]. I investigated sexual harassment many, many times. I lived a very cautious life.”

title: Sen. Bernie Moreno says former son-in-law Max Miller shouldn’t serve in Congress following abuse allegations
summary: Rep. Max Miller, R-Ohio, denied allegations that he abused the senator’s daughter and chastised him for speaking out.
story: Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, said Sunday on X that his former son-in-law Rep. Max Miller “needs to seek professional help” and should not serve in Congress following domestic abuse allegations made by Miller’s ex-wife, Emily Moreno, the senator’s daughter.

“Out of concern for the safety of my family, I hoped to keep this matter private but Max Miller’s increasingly erratic and dangerous behavior has made that impossible,” Moreno said in a lengthy post to X, the first time he has discussed his daughter’s divorce and the allegations against Miller in depth.
“As he has admitted privately, Max Miller needs serious psychological help,” Moreno continued. “He is a danger to my daughter, and I hold my breath every minute he has custody of my granddaughter.”
The senator said in the post, “If there are any basic standards of character required to hold elected office, Max Miller fails them.”

“He should not serve in the House of Representatives,” Moreno said. “I believe Max Miller needs to seek professional help to end the clear pattern of abuse he has left in his wake. I believe he should not be free to continue endangering others until he does.”

Miller’s office did not immediately respond to NBC News’ request for comment on Moreno’s post. Miller, though, responded on X to Moreno’s post, writing, “If my daughter said the same thing to me, I personally wouldn’t wait two years before holding him accountable.”
“You know this isn’t true and the only reason you are speaking out now is to hide from your own media circus,” he said. “This is all political.”
The senator’s post comes after Miller, R-Ohio, said in a livestream Saturday that he would not drop his re-election bid and vigorously denied allegations that he abused his ex-wife.
“I’m not getting out of this race, and I’m winning in November, and I’ll be back in the 120th,” Miller said, referring to the 120th Congress.

Last month, the outlet Mother Jones detailed allegations of Miller behaving violently toward multiple women, being verbally abusive and having used drugs. The outlet said its report was based on more than 2,000 pages of court filings and police reports obtained through public records requests. Mother Jones reported that a spokesperson for Miller declined to respond to questions the outlet sent to his lawyers but pointed to Miller’s previous denials of violence against women.

Emily Moreno has accused Miller of throwing hot water on her, throwing her against a wall and holding a gun to her head, according to police reports. Their daughter has also suffered a broken collarbone and bruising, the cause of which was disputed but investigated by police in February 2026. He has denied the allegations and has not faced criminal charges related to her claims.

In the more than 15-minute livestream, Miller tried to dismiss his ex-wife’s claims, saying that she did not go to the hospital or police after an incident in which she alleged he physically assaulted her. He also pointed to their interactions over the following days.

“Ask yourself: If I had assaulted her, would she have offered to cook me dinner six days later?” he said. “Would she have invited me to spend an afternoon at the playground with her and our daughter? Would she have written that we were in a friendlier place?”
Miller also released a series of documents and audio recordings he said back up his claims.

Emily Moreno’s spokesperson Stefan Mychajliw said in a statement that it was “shameful that Max Miller decided to go on a bizarre and lie-filled rant about his ex-wife to desperately try to save his political career.”

“There is a documented trove of evidence that Miller has a history of violent and dangerous behavior and no amount of victim shaming will change that,” Mychajliw said. “It is despicable and abhorrent that Miller lied on an unhinged and humiliating video for their daughter to watch one day.”
Mychajliw said that Moreno is “confident that justice will prevail in court.”
Emily Moreno’s lawyer Subodh Chandra added in a statement, “When adverse parties in litigation are setting themselves on fire, I do not provide them with a fire extinguisher.”
Miller sued Emily Moreno this year, alleging defamation.

In 2021, Miller filed a defamation lawsuit against former White House press secretary Stephanie Grisham after she alleged that a White House staffer physically abused her. She did not initially use Miller’s name, but he identified himself in the lawsuit. Grisham alleged that her boyfriend at the time was violent with her. Miller voluntarily dropped the lawsuit in 2023.
This year, Grisham sued Miller, alleging that he broke the nondisclosure agreement signed after he sued her.

title: Former Texas Rep. Kay Granger dies at 83
summary: Republican former Rep. Kay Granger of Texas has died, lawmakers announced Sunday.
story: Republican former Rep. Kay Granger of Texas has died, lawmakers announced Sunday.
Granger, who served on Capitol Hill for 28 years and chaired the House Appropriations Committee, was 83.
House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., announced Granger’s death on X, calling her “a dear friend who will be greatly missed.”

“Throughout her career, she broke barriers for women in public service. She was the first woman to serve as Mayor of Fort Worth, the first Republican woman elected to represent Texas in the U.S. House of Representatives, and the first Republican woman to chair the House Appropriations Committee,” Johnson wrote.

In December 2024, The Dallas Express reported that Granger, who had not cast a vote since July of that year and had announced in 2023 that she would not seek re-election, was residing in an assisted living facility. Her son later told The Dallas Morning News that she was experiencing “dementia issues.”
Current and former members of Congress offered their condolences on social media Sunday night.
House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., called her an “Iron Lady,” adding on X, “I’m grateful to have called her a friend.”
Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, said Granger “lived a life of historic firsts.”
“For nearly three decades, she championed North Texas, our Armed Forces, and a strong national defense,” Cruz wrote. “We are praying for her family and all who loved her.”
Rep. Rosa DeLauro, D-Conn., who preceded Granger as Appropriations chair, said she was “deeply saddened,” calling it “an honor to serve alongside her.”

“Throughout our years serving together on the Appropriations Committee, we worked through difficult challenges with mutual respect and honesty,” DeLauro said in a statement. “At every step of her career, she earned the respect of Members on both sides of the aisle through her steady leadership and deep belief in the importance of Congress fulfilling its constitutional responsibility to invest in the American people.”

title: Dominic Sessa Doesn’t Idolize Anthony Bourdain. It’s Why He Could Play Him
