It was so innocent and genuine,” Haynes says. “I love how kids are just unapologetically themselves, and seeing her confidently tell Karol G that her favorite song was ‘Dai Dai’ by Shakira was such a sweet moment I’ll never forget.”
And it was a memorable night for Karol as she became the first female solo artist to headline a show at Rogers Stadium.

The “Latina Foreva” singer kicked off her “Viajando Por El Mundo TropiTour” on July 27 in Chicago, with fans calling the show a celebration of culture, fawning over her sensational outfits and band on stage.
Just in the past days while on tour, Karol announced her new single, “Matadora,” as well as a new album “No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto.”

During her Toronto concert, she revealed that it will be released on Friday, Aug. 7. The cover art was also unveiled on the screens. She will continue touring across North America, Latin America and Europe, marking her largest live production yet.

title: Trump calls Iranian leadership ‘extremely duplicitous’ after Tehran denies new talks will start Monday
summary: President Donald Trump branded the Iranian regime “unbelievably duplicitous,” saying Iranian officials asked for talks on ending the war only to announce that no discussions would be held.
story: President Donald Trump branded the Iranian regime “unbelievably duplicitous,” saying Iranian officials asked for talks on ending the war only to announce that no discussions would be held.

Trump had earlier said that the United States and Iran will hold new discussions Monday afternoon, after he called off intense new strikes to allow for a deal on the Strait of Hormuz and Tehran’s nuclear program.
However, Iran said it was not currently holding talks with the U.S. but was in discussions with Oman over a temporary safe route through the strait.

“We currently do not have negotiations with America,” and Iran had no plans to host foreign delegations or send negotiators abroad in the coming days, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei told reporters.

Trump later took to Truth Social, where he wrote: “Iranian Leadership is unbelievably duplicitous! They ask for a meeting, some would say ‘beg,’ talks begin, with more scheduled in the immediate future, and they say, openly and proudly, that they’re not having any discussions, that nothing is being talked about, and they’re only dealing with ‘Oman.’”
Iran did not immediately respond to his comments.
Trump later told reporters at the White House after his post on Truth Social that talks with Iran were taking place.

“They’re going on right now. It’s an amazing thing we have a little problem with Iran because we have many talks, and we’ll say we have or we don’t have. You know, we’re straight about it, but they deny it,” Trump said. “But they’re not denying it now. They just put out a statement, not denying it.”
Trump also told reporters that the Strait of Hormuz will be open to marine traffic tomorrow.

“We’re talking about the strait, the opening of the strait, having it open literally by tomorrow, completely open, and that’s phase one,” Trump said, noting that the second phase of talks would focus on Iran’s nuclear program.
Time is running out for Iran to make a deal, according to Trump.
“This is a last chance for them to sign a good document,” Trump said and added, “I want to give them every last chance before decapitation,” Trump said.
Trump had said Sunday that he agreed to call off the attacks amid what he said were the “perimeters of a deal” that would include resuming shipping through the key global trade route.

Speaking on Air Force One, Trump said the canceled strikes were going to be “the biggest attack since World War II.” The president said that the U.S. was “holding” what would have been a “massive attack,” but that it could still take place “anytime we want.”
Trump, however, said that Iran does not have a deadline to come to an agreement.

title: Hackers targeted municipal water systems in 7 states this week, FBI says
summary: Cyberattacks targeting municipal water systems have been reported in at least seven states this week, prompting the FBI and the Environmental Protection Agency to warn utilities nationwide that hackers are trying to disrupt critical water infrastructure.
story: Cyberattacks targeting municipal water systems have been reported in at least seven states this week, prompting the FBI and the Environmental Protection Agency to warn utilities nationwide that hackers are trying to disrupt critical water infrastructure.

In a public service announcement Thursday, the agencies said water and wastewater utilities have reported incidents to the FBI, with some malicious activity degrading water operations. The announcement does not name the states.

The warning comes after hackers targeted more than 30 municipal water facilities in Minnesota in an attack that had hallmarks of Iranian meddling, according to a law enforcement official. It is still under investigation.

A spokesperson for Minnesota’s information technology services agency said Thursday there was no indication the breaches contaminated any municipal water supplies. The federal Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency said in a separate alert that some larger attacks on water infrastructure had “resulted in boil water notices and sustained manual operations,” though it did not say where.

Minnesota officials and the U.S. government have not publicly attributed the malicious activity in the state to a specific actor. Likewise, the FBI and the EPA did not identify a culprit behind the breaches in the other states.
Add NBC News to Google
Add NBC News to Google
President Donald Trump, speaking to reporters Friday at Camp David, blamed Minnesota’s leaders and Gov. Tim Walz, who was the Democratic vice presidential nominee in the 2024 election.

“I think I blame it on Minnesota because they’re grossly incompetent,” Trump said. “I would blame it on Minnesota and the governor, the corrupt governor of Minnesota. They like to say, ‘Oh, it’s Iran.’ Iran should be so lucky. Iran’s got bigger problems than worrying about Minnesota.”

In response to a request for comment, Walz said in part: “Trump knows exactly who is responsible for this attack, and knows that other states were hit too. This is what modern warfare looks like, and it further illustrates there’s no plan to win a war with Iran.”
Michigan and Rapid City, South Dakota also confirmed cyber incidents involving water systems.

In a statement, a spokesman for Michigan’s environment and energy department said the state received “a small number of reports ... indicating activity consistent with” the hacking described by federal agencies. Rapid City, meanwhile, said it “experienced a cyber incident” involving one of its list stations, which is used as part of the city’s wastewater system.

Thursday’s federal advisory said the malicious cyber actors, or MCAs, targeted specific brands of control systems used by municipal water utilities, though the FBI and the EPA urged operators of all systems to take precautions.

Earlier this week, the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources issued a bulletin to water contacts in the state, saying  intelligence officials believed that “systems within Wisconsin may be susceptible to connections from malicious cyber actors.”
“This leads us to believe that the cyber threat is ongoing in Wisconsin and requires immediate action to prevent potentially serious impacts to our systems,” the bulletin said.

A Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources spokesperson emphasized that intelligence officials in the state “had not yet confirmed that systems in Wisconsin have had connections but are concerned that they might be susceptible to connections from malicious cyber actors.”
In the warning, Wisconsin said that Minnesota had reported that hackers managed to drop system pressures, which in “several incidents triggered alarms and prompted a response from law enforcement.”
In an email, the spokesperson for Minnesota’s information technology agency disputed Wisconsin’s characterizations of the attack and its observed impacts.
“Minnesota has not reported that threat actors lowered pressure across multiple water systems or that pressure changes prompted a law enforcement response,” said the spokesperson, Emily Zimmer.
The agencies said the hackers remotely accessed internet-facing devices, changed IP addresses and passwords, and caused utilities to lose monitoring and control capabilities.

The federal advisory calls on system operators to remove programmable logic controllers, or PLCs, from direct internet exposure by putting them behind secure gateways and firewalls; use strong passwords; and limit communications between authorized control system devices through access control lists.

“Attribution requires careful analysis of technical evidence alongside broader national and international threat intelligence, and our federal partners are best positioned to lead that work,” Zimmer, the spokesperson for Minnesota’s information technology agency, said.

The breach in Minnesota happened just days after U.S. officials publicly warned that Iran-backed hackers were targeting the nation’s critical infrastructure amid the escalating military conflict between Washington and Tehran.

In a public advisory July 22, CISA, as well as the FBI and other federal agencies, urged companies to boost their defenses, saying Tehran-linked hackers were trying to breach online automated devices used to manage infrastructure systems.
U.S. intelligence agencies have also cautioned that Iran is increasingly able and willing to carry out aggressive cyber operations and that it tried to target water systems in 2023.

Bryson Bort, the founder of the cybersecurity company Scythe and an expert in industrial control system security, said the FBI’s disclosures this week underscore the need for more public awareness of the risks posed by infrastructure breaches.
“We need to be prepared,” Bort said. “Attacks like this illustrate that there are folks who mean the U.S. harm today.”

title: U.S. agrees to pause attacks on Iran subject to ‘rapidly’ making deal, Trump says
summary: The deal would include reopening the Strait of Hormuz and ending Tehran’s “nuclear threat,” the president said.
story: The U.S. has agreed to pause attacks on Iran, President Donald Trump said Saturday, amid what he said were the “perimeters of a deal” that would include the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.

“We have just been asked by Iran, and other Middle Eastern Countries, to hold off any attack in that the perimeters of a deal has been agreed to,” Trump said in a post on Truth Social. “This would include the Immediate, Complete, and Total OPENING OF THE HORMUZ STRAIT, and an end to Iran’s  nuclear threat.”
The president said the U.S. was “locked and loaded and ready to go” but that he agreed to cancel attacks “subject to being able to rapidly make a DEAL.”
He added that Israel, the U.S. partner in the war with Iran, “joins me in this commitment.”
“Get to work, everybody, and get it DONE,” Trump said of a possible new agreement.

The statement came after the State Department on Saturday urged Americans across the Middle East to consider leaving the region or be prepared to depart on short notice. It also warned of flight disruptions and security risks as the conflict with Iran appeared to be escalating.

Trump earlier threatened Iran with additional attacks, saying Friday that the U.S. will be “hitting them very hard,” while Iran has vowed to “punish” the U.S. and both nations traded what some U.S. officials described as “heavy” strikes.
Responding to Trump’s announcement, Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., told “Meet the Press” Sunday that the president should not trust Iran’s word.
Asked why a fresh deal would be different when the memorandum of understanding signed in June failed, he told moderator Kristen Welker: “Well, it may not be.”
“We only have three choices: escalate, retreat and come home, or maintain the status quo. I would maintain the status quo as long as I could,” he said.
Iran’s acting minister of defense, Majid Ibn al-Reza, meanwhile said that U.S. remarks should be viewed as “psychological and cognitive warfare.”
He said on X that the threat of further strikes would be taken “as the basis for increasing readiness, strengthening deterrence, and enhancing our own power.”

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, a key regional player, spoke with Trump by phone Saturday. According to the Saudi state news agency, he told him that dialogue was needed to de-escalate Middle East tensions, and expressed concerns over plans for new strikes against Iran.
The State Department issued fresh security guidance Saturday for Americans in the region.

“Americans currently in the Middle East should exercise caution and heightened vigilance and should be prepared for flight cancellations, periodic airspace closures, and potential travel disruptions,” the State Department said. “Some airlines in the region have postponed resumption of earlier flight schedules; others have cancelled some routes. Americans in the region should consider departing, or be prepared to depart should there be escalation.”
The State Department also urged Americans to reconsider travel bans to or through the region.
The warning was distributed through U.S. embassies in the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Oman, Qatar and Saudi Arabia.

The agency posted a nearly identical statement earlier this month, but that bulletin did not urge Americans to prepare to leave the Middle East or to reconsider upcoming trips, reflecting Washington’s growing concern that the conflict could widen.
On Saturday, the Kuwait army said its air defense systems intercepted drone attacks from Iran.

“Kuwaiti air defenses are currently engaging hostile drone attacks following the Iranian aggression. The General Staff of the Army notes that any explosions heard are a result of air defense systems intercepting the hostile attacks,” the army said.

Earlier in the week, the U.S. military confirmed it had executed a “heavy wave of strikes” on Iran, hours after Fox News reported that the president in a phone call had vowed to “beat the f-----g s--- out of” the country.
Trump has grown increasingly exasperated with the state of the war, one Trump ally told NBC News.
“There was not a real strategy for how long or what they should do to get to the endpoint,” the ally said.
The conflict has now entered its sixth month, despite Trump’s repeated early predictions that the war would resolve itself “shortly.”
The protracted conflict has led to soaring oil prices globally and rising gas prices in the U.S.
There was a brief reprieve from fighting in June when the U.S. and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding outlining the process for talks to end the war.
But in early July, Trump declared a ceasefire to be “over,” and the countries resumed striking targets in the Middle East.

title: At least 86 dead after migrants rush into Spanish territory from Morocco
summary: Spain was scrambling Friday to contain a sudden border crisis after tens of thousands of people rushed into its North African territory, with dozens killed and political shock waves spreading across Europe.
story: Spain was scrambling Friday to contain a sudden border crisis after tens of thousands of people rushed into its North African territory, with dozens killed and political shock waves spreading across Europe.

The dramatic events were “a violation of Spain’s territorial sovereignty,” Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said on a hurried visit to Ceuta, a tiny Mediterranean city at the tip of Africa that shares a border with Morocco.

Authorities in Ceuta told Sky News on Saturday that 86 people have died following the incident. The Spanish Interior Ministry earlier told NBC News that some 50,000 people had entered Ceuta on Thursday from Morocco, more than half of the city’s usual population.
Around half of that number had returned Friday, the Interior Ministry said.

title: Iran vows to ‘punish the aggressor today’ after U.S. unleashes ‘heavy wave’ of strikes
summary: The conflict appeared to draw in new countries, as Egypt confirmed that a drone hit two natural gas vessels at one of its ports.
story: Iran vowed to “punish” the United States on Thursday after the American military said it had completed a “heavy wave of strikes” overnight, the latest retaliation for an attack by Tehran on U.S. forces in the Middle East.
The renewed fighting shattered a brief period of calm that had seen the two sides engage with a push to revive diplomatic efforts and stave off dramatic new escalation.

But President Donald Trump said the U.S. would hit Iran hard after its attack on an American base in Jordan. And the powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) signaled the flare-up would not end there, warning early Thursday that “the aggressor will be punished today” following the U.S. strikes.
Jordan said it intercepted a new barrage from Iran, while Kuwait said an Iranian strike hit a building belonging to a Chinese company, killing one worker.
There were also signs that the war was again expanding and drawing in new countries, raising the stakes for the region and the global economy.
After Saudi Arabia joined the U.S. in striking Iran-backed militants in Iraq, Egypt confirmed Thursday that a drone ignited fires on two natural gas vessels at the Mediterranean port of Damietta.

Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman met with Trump and Vice President JD Vance on Wednesday to relay a message from Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman that the kingdom is not looking to escalate the war with Iran, according to a source familiar with the matter.
The separate meetings came within 24 hours of the joint U.S. and Saudi strikes against Iran-backed militants in Iraq, according to a White House official.
The discussions were first reported by Axios.

In his meetings, the defense minister conveyed that the Iranian militias had crossed a line and Saudi Arabia will not tolerate anyone attacking their civilian infrastructure or energy facilities, the source said. He also emphasized that the strikes were to demonstrate Saudi Arabia’s capacity to defend itself when needed and not an indication of support for escalation.
The Saudis believe that any escalation would involve unknown risks and likely prolong the war, which is not the path they desire for the region, the source said.

It was not immediately clear who was behind the drone strikes — on a U.S.-owned floating storage facility and a Greek-owned tanker — in Egypt but an attack there by Iran would mark a significant new expansion of the conflict to a key U.S. ally and mediator. It would also highlight the broader risk to the world’s energy supplies from the difficulty in resolving the conflict.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Thursday that Egypt is an “important friend” in a post on X.

“Egypt is an important friend and partner in the region, and its security is of utmost importance to us,” he wrote. “We must all be vigilant against Israeli plots and false-flag operations designed to undermine regional peace.”
Asked if Iran was responsible for the Egypt attack during an Oval Office event Wednesday, Trump said that he had been briefed on the incident and that “it’s a little more of the same.”
“It’s going to be straightening out,” he added, without expanding on what exactly he meant. “In the meantime, we’re going to be hitting them very hard because it’s our turn to hit them.”
Trump also vowed Wednesday to “beat the f---ing s--- out of” Iran after its Tuesday attack on American forces, according to Fox News, which cited a phone call with the president.

title: U.S. strikes Iran after Trump reportedly issues menacing new threat
summary: The fighting shattered a brief period of calm after weeks of escalation between the U.S. and Iran over the strategic Strait of Hormuz.
story: The U.S. military attacked Iran on Wednesday after President Donald Trump vowed to “beat the f---ing s--- out of” the country, according to Fox News, following new attacks on American forces in the Middle East.
“They’re going to get a beating,” Trump said, according to Fox’s chief foreign correspondent, Trey Yingst.
U.S. Central Command said a “heavy wave of strikes” had been completed at 10 p.m. ET, two hours after they began.
The strikes on dozens of targets “aimed to further diminish threats posed by Iran and its proxies to American forces, commercial shipping, and neighboring Gulf countries,” the command said on X.
The comments followed what the U.S. described as a “surprise attack,” which prompted Saudi Arabia and the U.S. to retaliate against a Tehran-backed militia in Iraq.

Iran had suspended its attacks amid a renewed push to reach a deal with the U.S., but it warned this week that it would not allow Washington to dictate the “timing of war and peace” and maintained that the Strait of Hormuz was “closed.”
The sudden return of hostilities shattered the relative calm that had descended on Iran for several days after the U.S. paused daily strikes on the Islamic Republic to make room for peace talks.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said it launched strikes on a U.S. air base and military central command center in Jordan, state-run Nour News agency reported early Wednesday local time. Its navy also struck three oil tankers that it said were “in violation” of its blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, according to the state-run news agency IRNA.

U.S. Central Command, or CENTCOM, said on X that it had thwarted an “attempted surprise attack” on forces based in the Middle East around 5:45 p.m. Tuesday. All Iranian missiles were intercepted, it said, but troops remained “vigilant and at a high state of readiness.”

Just hours later, CENTCOM said it had launched “precision strikes” in Iraq alongside the Saudi armed forces against “Iran-aligned terrorists” that it said the IRGC had directed to attack U.S. forces and Saudi energy infrastructure.

title: K-pop group BTS won’t submit its music for Grammy Awards
summary: “I hope that music can be heard and loved for what it is, rather than being divided by region or language,” the group said in a statement.
story: K-pop sensation BTS said Wednesday that it will not submit its music for consideration at the 2027 Grammy Awards, citing concerns over category divisions.
The seven members — RM, Jimin, V, Suga, Jungkook, Jin and j-Hope — uploaded the same statement to their individual Instagram accounts.
“We have decided not to enter the Grammys this year,” a translation of the message read. “I hope that music can be heard and loved for what it is, rather than being divided by region or language.”

The hugely popular group from South Korea was widely expected to be nominated for some of the Recording Academy’s top accolades at the 69th Grammy Awards — including album of the year. The boyband’s most recent album, “Arirang,” has been one of the bestselling records of the year.
The album’s lead single, “Swim,” was a Billboard Hot 100 No. 1 hit in the United States.

Under the new categorizations, “Swim” might have been excluded from competing for best Asian pop music performance, one of the five new categories the Recording Academy announced last month. The new award categories were sold as an effort to boost inclusivity.

While a lot of BTS’ songs are in Korean, the lead track is mostly sung in English. A rulebook for the Grammy Awards specifies that the recordings for the new award “must feature meaningful use of one or more Asian languages.”
“An Asian language should play a significant role within the song in bilingual or multilingual structures such that the recording is identifiable with that language,” the rulebook reads.
Grammys CEO Harvey Mason Jr. said in a statement Wednesday that he was saddened by the group’s decision “but as a music creator, I understand and respect their decision.”
He said the Asian Pop category was created to celebrate “the depth, diversity and extraordinary growth of pop artistry coming out of Asia.”
“More categories mean more artists’ work is recognized. It’s never to divide, but to expand who is recognized by our 15,000 Grammy voters,” Mason said.
He noted that submitting music in a specific genre category doesn’t exclude artists from also submitting and being considered  general categories, such as Song of the Year.
Mason said the Grammys will “continue to listen to the global music community and work to honor and celebrate all the artists whose music moves the world.”

BTS, which formed in 2013 and has been compared to The Beatles, has previously performed at the Grammys and was the first K-pop act to receive a Grammy nomination. It has earned five nominations but so far hasn’t won.

BTS stands for the Korean phrase “Bangtan Sonyeondan,” which translates to “Bulletproof Boy Scouts.” The band has a huge global following and recently performed in the United States during the World Cup final’s halftime show.
On Wednesday, the group thanked its fans for their support.
“Thank you to Army and everyone who is always with us,” the band said.

title: At least 13 killed in Japan earthquake as rescuers search for survivors in a ‘race against time’
summary: Multiple people were missing a day after a magnitude-7.1 quake struck Kumamoto prefecture, partially collapsing buildings.
story: At least 13 people have been killed in southwestern Japan after a magnitude-7.1 earthquake, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said Wednesday, as rescuers searched for people trapped in collapsed buildings, including a shopping mall.

“Even now, there are people waiting to be rescued, and this is a race against time. We will marshal all available resources on the ground to save and rescue as many people as possible,” Takaichi told reporters in Tokyo.

The quake struck Tuesday afternoon in Kumamoto prefecture on Japan’s southern main island of Kyushu at a relatively shallow depth of 6 miles, prompting tsunami warnings and evacuation from coastal areas. The epicenter was about 12 miles south of the city of Kumamoto, which has a population of about 700,000.

While the tsunami warning was lifted shortly after, the quake caused extensive damage throughout the prefecture, including to historic buildings such as Kumamoto Castle, a popular tourist site that is still under repair from another deadly quake in the same area in 2016.
It also ruptured roads and left thousands of homes without power, with officials warning residents to beware of heatstroke as temperatures reach well into the 90s.

title: Major earthquake rocks southern Japan, injuring dozens
summary: The earthquake, which had an epicenter in the southwest part of the country, was measured at magnitude 6.8 and a depth of 10 kilometers, or just over 6 miles.
story: A 6.8-magnitude earthquake rocked southern Japan on Tuesday, forcing hundreds of thousands of people to evacuate and prompting the collapse of several buildings, including a shopping mall.
Japanese officials instructed roughly 300,000 people in the country’s southern Kumamoto prefecture to seek shelter at evacuation centers.
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said Wednesday morning local time that 13 people have been found dead and many other people were injured or still missing as rescue work continued overnight.

The Japan Meteorological Agency said the earthquake, with a preliminary magnitude of 7.1 and depth of just over 6 miles, was at the highest end of the seismic intensity scale. The U.S. Geological Survey later revised its measurement to magnitude 6.8. Its epicenter was about 12 miles south of Kumamoto, central Kyushu island’s largest city, with a population of around 700,000, according to officials.

The Japanese Cabinet Office’s disaster management division said the earthquake struck around 4:27 p.m. local time (3:27 a.m. ET), with a tsunami advisory issued for the Ariake and Yatsushiro seas minutes later. The warning was later lifted, state broadcaster NHK reported.

An unknown number of people were trapped in a shopping mall, according to fire officials, who said an explosion had been heard on the building’s second floor. Twenty to 30 mall employees were unaccounted for, NHK reported.

Commercial broadcaster TBS quoted local police as saying “quite a few” people are believed to have been killed after the explosion. A second broadcaster, Fuji TV, said that multiple deaths had been confirmed at the mall.
Add NBC News to Google
Add NBC News to Google
State broadcaster NHK carried footage of almost a dozen fire trucks in the facility’s parking lot. Images also showed the mall’s collapsed ceilings and facade and a debris-littered road.
Several other buildings were also damaged, video from the region showed. At least 12 houses collapsed, and at least 50 people were injured.

Aerial footage from NHK showed that a chimney at a Nippon Paper Industries plant in Yatsushiro, a city in the Kumamoto prefecture, had partially collapsed. Local police said that several people who work at the plant are unaccounted for.
“We are gathering information on whether there are any casualties, but we are concerned because we cannot reach them,” a spokesperson for the plant told NHK.

A verified video from the city showed that a rupture on the Kyushu Expressway had trapped vehicles. NHK showed aerial images of an elevated stretch of the highway where two sections had become misaligned.
Train services around the Kyushu island were suspended, rail operator JR Kyushu said.
Takaichi said in a statement that 300 service members were being dispatched to the disaster zone.

“The government will spare no effort in emergency disaster response measures, with the highest priority placed on saving lives and rescue operations led by local police and fire departments,” her office said in a statement.
“Strong tremors, earthquakes of similar intensity may continue to occur over approximately the next week,” the statement added.

title: Search for North Carolina woman Liz Waddell is still a missing person case, Grenada police say
summary: Grenadian police said their nearly week-old search for a missing North Carolina woman is still active, with hopes of finding the swimmer alive.
story: Grenadian police said Tuesday that their nearly week-old search for a missing North Carolina woman is still active, with hopes of finding the swimmer alive.
Elizabeth “Liz” Waddell, a 44-year-old Cary resident, was last seen going out for a swim at Grand Anse Beach on Wednesday, the Royal Grenada Police Force said.

“At this time, the matter continues, continues to be treated as a missing person investigation,” acting Commissioner of Police Randy Connaught told reporters Tuesday. “I repeat, at this time, the matter continues to be treated as a missing person.”
Add NBC News to Google
Add NBC News to Google
Surveillance cameras captured Waddell walking on a jetty near the water at 11:36 a.m. the morning she went missing, Connaught said.
She went into the water at 11:51 a.m. and more footage captured her swimming under the jetty at 12:04 p.m., the police official said.
Witnesses have told investigators they later saw Waddell in the open water, police said.
Waddell’s traveling partner was captured on surveillance cameras on the beach at 12:46 p.m. and she reported the swimmer missing to police at 5:50 p.m., Connaught added.
“There is nothing questionable about her account of the investigations and we continue to receive cooperation from her,”  Connaught said of the traveling companion.
Even though Waddell hasn’t been seen in nearly six days, police said they still seek to rescue her.
“It is our hope that Elizabeth will be found and found alive and well,” Connaught said. “The Royal Grenada Police Force remains equally hopeful that she will be safe and that she is safe.”
Local police had been appealing to fishermen, boat operators and residents along the southern coastline to keep their eyes peeled for medium-build woman with short blond hair.
Waddell and her friend first arrived in Grenada, the island nation in the eastern Caribbean Sea that’s about 100 miles north of Venezuela, on July 11.
The missing woman’s husband has since come to the island to help in the search effort, officials said.

“Any bit of information will do at this time, and we do hope that we can locate Elizabeth very soon,” Connaught said. “Again, we empathize with the family, relatives and friends, and we are hopeful that Elizabeth will be found alive. Thank you.”
